MY DEAF. NELLIE',

There are some very _ be seen now the summer is rapi . d .•i. , • 14951 is W.•' smart little serge coat a.'ço finished with a stitched ban :All re o,sterr; ing over any shirt or blo2 '6, and 'the donbld., breasted coat having adir% ".7op Ohllar and ratiiki,!; ! full sleeves drawn int:3' ti. t Cuffi. In a pale' shade of blue it looks very pretty, but for hard, every-day wear darker colours are, of course, , better. By the way, the hat which is worn with thß costume is particularly worthy of note, for it has a wide. brim, which makes a good protection frem the sun; and is prettily trimmed with a scarf - of blue and white checked silk, drawn at the side into a loose bow with fringed ends. It is lined, too, with silk, and therd is a little rouleatt of velvet to make it fit comfortably and closely on the

Stylish millinery is another feature of th, fashions now that beautiful weather is eornio,. after so much of the wet. I saw a beautiful Ike dress the other day which is in the very latest fashion, for complete tkesses of lace are among the season's most fascinating novelties. The gown is made of pale rose-pink glacd silk, veiled with creamy chiffon, which is gauged at intervals on the yoke and sleeves. At tho t..dge of the skirt there are three accordion-pleated frills of chiffon, bordered with tiny ruchings of the same. These make the clinging skirt stand out full at the bottom. The lower part of the bodice and the back and sides of the skirt are entirely covered with creamy lace, which is made all in one piece to the required shape, and has only to .be mounted on the tmderdress. These exquisite lace robes are made in various other shapes as well, and some of them completely cover the dress, as they have long sleeves, entire bodices, and even basques and epaulettes, as well as long skirts, in various shapes. Dust-proof serges and alpacas make delightful travelling dresses.

The most practical of hats is of rustic straw trimmed with bows of black velvet ribbon and variegated roses or ?ilk poppies. Manillas, Tuscan and Panama straws are ever dear to the heart of dark women, whom they suit admirably, and many of the cheap straws boast of every conceivable colouring save turquoise-bluo,. which is never a success except in the better qualities. &rings are to be seen in the milliners' shop windows, but it would seem that Frenchwomen alone have the faculty of making them look becoming. Save for elderly matrons they have not caught on here. One of the most delightful features of the summer are the large collars and vests of tucked muslin, trimmed with insertion and lace'.
One pretty afternoon gown I have seen is of pinkish mauve foulard, with little black rings all over it. The skirt is trimmr ' with shaped frills,

which are edged with .narrow ruchings of fine, black lace, and these form a tablier trimming on the left side. The draperies of the bodice open over a vest of soft white Venetian, with a yoke of gauged white chiffon, and the wide collar-revers, which reach over the top of the sleeves, are also faced with white ghiffon, and have a double row of black lace ruching at the edge. Ruchings of black lace aleo appear at the wrists and throat. With this is worn a hat of fancy white satin straw, trimmed with white glace silk and clusters of mauve and pink hydrangeas and foliage. Hats are all the rage now, however. I may say that one I have bought this week is a very becoming hat of yellow fancy satin straw, trimmed with soft folds of black tulle, which is edged with fine black lace and rows of narrow black ribbon velvet. On the left side there are some long black ostrich feathers, and nother black- ostrich tip appears under the brim on the hair. Soft strings of black tulle tie loosely round the neck into a pretty bow under the chin.
Your loving JENNIE.

POTATO SALAD.—PIa(Ie on a flat dish a small mound of boiled potatoes sliced while hot; add immediately a French dressing of fur tablospoon- fuls of melted latitteF; half a teaspDonful cf salt and two tablespoonfuls of vioe-ar. Pour it slowly over the potatoes. and doe the top with black pepper. If the dressing is added to the iiced potatoes while ibis hot, when cold it will not turn dark.

RlCE.—Wash one cupful of rice, put it into three and a half cupfuls of boiling water, and let it Loil rapidly for 15 minutes. Cooked in this way every kernel should be perfect and stand apart from the rest. The water drained off from toe rice in the first boiling may be used in making soup.

"WOMEN'S CHAT." The gifts pre3ented to Her Majesty, on the occasion of her eightieth birthday, have formed almost as large a collection as was the case at the last Jubilee, and an idea is entertained of an exhibition in London. The most magnificent of the presents have come from the Indian Princes, and include many rich specimens of Oriente' and lacquer work. Among members of the Queen's family, all gifts naust be of home manufacture, and na exception to the rule has been made on this lest auspic- ious occasion. Quite the smallest of Her Majesty's des- cendaets have been busy for weeks past, making " something tor Grannie," and these little items must have looked not a little curious m‘xed up with magni- ficent and costly gifts. But the Queen always treasures these efforts, which are duly labelled and put away, or kept in constant use, as the case may be. Kensington Palace, which was opened to the public on the eightieth anniversary of Her Majesty's birthdav,was completed in 1696, the cost amounting to about £90,000. The gardens, intended only for the pedestrian, are con- spicuous for presenting one immense and almost contin- uous mass of shade. beneath the noble avenues, and clumps of fine old trees. King William HI bought the gardens, which at that time only occupied 28 acres. Queen Anne enlarged them to 56 acres, and Queen Caro- line to their present extent. In this gardens the Queen was when a little girl, in the habit of taking al fresco breakfasts, with her mother, and probably it was then that Her Majt sty acquired that intense I we for the open air which has always been her characteristic. As everyone knows, it was at Kensington Palace on the 24th of May, 1819, that our Queen first saw the light. In this happy home the Princes Victoria passed her early youth, and it was here that the first !meting with Primes Albert took place, and it was here too she was first addressed as Queen. Kensington Palace is, also, the birthplace of the Duchess of York, but this fact seems to have escaped no ice so far. Prineess May was born in the room called the" nursery," in 1867. " tim," the sturdy Irish Airedale terrier, who recently had the honour of being presented to the Queen of Pad- dington Station, and who collects for the G.W.R., Widows and Orphans' Fund, is an indefatgiatle worker, having collected altogether nearly £4OO. In the pro- vinces are to be found several notable collecting dogs, but in London they are few and far between. This is a pity, for though the novelty of canine collectors has long since passed away, people wou'd still often give odd coppers to a dog when they would not subscribe to a fund in any other way. One rarely sees a Newfoundland now, which is a matter for regret. They are splendid fellows, and the expres4on in their glorious eyes would seem to indicate that they are in possession of all thevirtues, and require only opportunity to display them. Yorkshire terriers if small enough, are in great favour, but the correct size and weight are so microscopic, that the cost of the diminutive animal is very great. Schipperkes never really caught on with British women. There is some- thing so sly and cunning, even calculating in the expres- sion of their long and sharp nosed faces, that it is so difficult to like them. impossible to love them. According to Miss Maud Earl, the well-known artist, most dogs make nervous, excitable sitters, whi'e seme are relf-conscious. Collies for instance, she says, invari- ably pose themselves, when being painted. They know quite well that they are being admired and watched,and they are so accustomed to adulation, that they simply stand still and wait for it. A doe, as a rule, is required to sit two days, twelve hours in all. At the (ad of the two days the picture is complete. If he happens to be living within easy distance of the s udio however, Miss Earl has him there a third time, when the whole thing Is finished. Mrs. Cornwallis West has not enjoyed the best of health since her big party for the Chester races, which was henoured by tbe Prince of Wales, and is still at Ruthin Castle. But she hcpes to proceed to London for the latter part of the season should her own and her husband's health be sufficiently improved. Ruthin Castle is a fine old mansion erected on a portion of the old site where dioriginal castle stood. It is surrounded by a quaint Rae town, containing about 3,000 inhabit- ants, and an interesting church, which bas been well restored. Princess Henry of Pleas, the elder of Mrs. Cornwallis West's daughters, is an exceedingly lovely woman, and the younger, still unmarried, is very like her sister. Mrs. West, who in her day was a famous beauty, is a daughter of the Rev. F. Fitzpatrick, her mother being a sis'er of the late Lord Headfort. The London season grows shorter and shorter. Now it scarcely commences until Whitsuntide is over. The reason for this is that the smartest folks seldom leave the country before the end of February, and de not re- turn until the end of April. A decade since, compara- tively few went abroad forthe winter and if they did so, left in November or December, and returned in Febru- ary, the season being in full swing by the end of March. No great entertainment was given this year before Whit- suntide, and the late condition of affairs has been more noticeable than before, Tradespeople do not take kindly to this arrangement the loss to them being considerable. Evening wrap of the transparent persuasion, are among us, but up to the present time have been but little worn. The cold, damp nights we have experienced have not led us to yearn for such a form 61 covering, but rather for our cosy, fur-trimmed wraps!-- Possibly, when the sultry days and nights arrive, transparent cloaks will be in high favour, but they are never likely to be patroriised by any but wealthy women, being fragile and cettly in the extreme. One cloak I saw at a leading modistes the other day was draped about the shouldera with hand painted mauve and pale pink chiffon, from this drapery fell a transparent skirt of the pink chiffon, and the colter was of drawn pink and maute chiffon Outside, and drawn white inside. This sounds simple, but the figure at which it had just been sold was eighteen and a half guineas! And twice or three times was the utmost any woman could hope to don this fragile garment. Pointed belts have quite taken the place of straight ones, which is a happy idea as to all but the very slim, the po'nted variety is infinitely more becoming. The largo silver clasps which hail from Paris, come in reality from India, and are hand-wrought. Jewelled belts have quite disappeared for day wearattiose of plain ribbon finished with a neat clasp being the best wear. Sailor bats, like all others, are worn tilted forward. This tilt forward is a great improvement on the tilt backward, which obtained a few years ago. The milliner's halo at the back seemed to enlarge already ample countenances and to give to well marked features an air of exaggeration which was almost comic. Further, there is a rollicking air about a hat worn back, by a man, and the ,same characteristic seems Is invade it when a woman wears it the same way. Here is a capital way in which to utilise stale scraps of bread. Take half a pound of these, and crumble. Place them in a saucepan with a pint and a half of milk, boil them slowly, and beat them smooth. Add sugar to taste,fievour with lem 'f4 or vanilla. Beat the yolks of two eggs,add, beat ';' together and bake in a pie dish, Spread the top vette jam, whisk up the whites of the eggs to a stiff frech, and pile on top. Just set in the oven, then serve immediately. • " MADGE."

div.head: SANKEY BRIDGES WESLEYAN SUNDAY FCTIOOL
div.p: SANKEY BRIDGES WESLEYAN SUNDAY FCTIOOL
ANNIVERSARY SERVICES.

Very successfal anniversary services were held on Sunday in connection with the Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Sunaay School. This institution is si, li- sted in a thickly-populated district and is chiefi) carried on and supported by the working classes. The morning service on Sunday was conducted in the chapel. The Rev. J. Grange Bennett was the preacher, and he delivered a thoughtful diEcourse. Special hymns were sung by the children before a congregation which filled the limited sitting accommodation. For the afternoon and evening services, Parr Hall had been requisitioned, and this admirally met the exigences of the occasion. About 200 of the echool children were accom- modated on the platform,and attired in their Sunday best, they sweetly sang hymns and anthems. The children entered heartily into the singing, the girls especially distinguishing themselves. Mr. Brough the superin*.eudent of the sch 001, conducted with his accustomed ability, and he must have taken considerable pains in the practi( es to bring the singing to such a high state of efficiency. Mr. Tnomas Brough presided at the organ and the effectiveness of the musical accompaniments was considerably heightenrd by the performance of a small orchestral band. At the afternoon service solos were sung by Mr. Levi Richardson and Madame Conway. "Entreat me not "and the "Shepherd's Cradle song" were skilfully and feelingly interpreted Madame Conway. Mr. Richardson ale° sang two solos, his rendering of " Come unto Me," being par- ticularly fine. Tbe proceedings were presided over by Mr. Robert Garnett, J.P. , The Chairman delivered an interesting address directed chiefly for the benefit of the children. Be re- ferred to life as hello° a maxv,llous mystery and in the coulee of his remarks pictured it as a voyage. The children were those who were just starting from port, whilst those who were older were half-way over the seas, and others, like himself, were nearer the haven. They were all on the journey of life and could not be turned back. It was therefore necessary for them as intelligent persons to have a safe guide. No mariner would now think of undertaking a voyage without a mariner's com- pass, nor would a traveller think of going to a foreign country without endeavouring to know something about it. They mtvt; therefore prepare themselves. He wished them to remember the words of Christ which he spoke to His disciples " Seek first the Kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all things shall be added unto you." The Chairman proceeded to explain that the Kingdom of God was within them, and illustrated his remarks by referring to the examples set by persons who had had humble bvinnings, incluling George Whitfield. He scmetimee thought there were more opportunities than ever in the present day for young fellows to show the mettle they were made of and to distinguish themselves. There was no position in life in which young men were not exposed to many temptations. The Kingdom of God within them would enable them to see the right thing and would put loyalty into them. They were suffering from a want of loyalty in thee young men and also in their older men. There was a lack of loyalty in connection with their church sad their Sabbath schools. Let them not be carried away with everything that invited them. Life was before them and let them make the best of it. There were duties and obligations resting upon them which they could not depute to another. He would urge all to discharge them dili- gently and faithfully. They were not only respons- ible for what they did, but for what they left ucdone that they might have done. God's service was a reason- able one, and he had no doubt there were many who could testify to it. There was always a certain section of the community who tried to persuade others that re- ligious life was a mournfel lite. It was a joy lasting to eternity. That day pressnted a glorious opportunity for young men and young women to give their hearts to the Saviour, and to set out to follow him. There wss again a large congregation at the evening service, when the Rev. J. Grange Bennett preached. Madame Conway sang" Angels ever bright and fair." The children also rendered several hymns. The collec- tions for the day amounted to over £39.

DY JOHN BLOUNDELLE-BURTON, iuthor of "Fortune's my Foe," ."The Scourge of God," "Across the Salt Seas," "The Clash of Arms." "In the Day of Adversity," "A Gen- tleman Adventurer," "His Own Enemy," "Denounced," &c.
CHAPTER XIII. "SPARE HER! SPARE TIER!"

Mrs. Pooley, Bella and Gilbert sat alone in the saloon that night, the faces of the two women being 2.areworn and depressed in appearance, while, on that of the young naval officer, was a look, if not of consternation, at least of doubt and anxiety. Ilat all of them should present this appearance of perturbation was natural enough, because by this time it was impossible to suppose that any less than a calamity was impending over the Emperor of the Moon and all in her. Two more men, named Burgess and Trilby, had been attacked with blind- ness, while the negro, who had been the last survivor amongst the slaves, had himself now died. "It was," said Gilbert, who had come below to tell the ladies that which had happened above, since to keep silence on the subject was use Ass, in consequence of the turmoil in the ship which had ac- companied the poor creature's la* moments, "some- tiling awful. He died a raving maniac—nothing short of that. You heard his howls and yells after we had got him safely tied up ; we saw a sight that I, at least—and I should think everybody else —hope never to see again. Even roped as he was, his leaps and convulsions were someth' Thank God they soon came to an .:lerhe::" e he died of the exhaustion caused by 'his-'mm ••

"What is to become of us all ? " asked Mrs. Pooley feebly. "What? The ship moves only by the current ; my husband said just now that, if things go on and get worse, there will be none left to control her when the wind does come."

"The trouble is," said Gilbert, "that if they stake sail when the wind springs up, there may be none to take it in if it comes on too strong. And, at all events, it will be serious if more men are attacked. I have offered my servces in any capacity if wanted, and will serve either as officer or man if Captain Pooley will let me." Bella threw an admiring glance at her lover in approval of what she, in her own mind, probablyl-' considered his noble disinterestedness; then she said:
"But, surely all are not going to be attacked one after another in this way? And if so, uncle can't possibly think of trying to get to Bombay when the wind does i;Ome.

"I have suggested the same thing to him that Fagg did this afternoon, namely, the Seychelles. They're all right, and the climate is first-rate for the tropics. He says, however, he will see what happens by the time we get a wind. He won't give in if no more men are attacked."

Meanwhile, even as he spoke, each of the trio were occupied with thoughts which they would not have cared to put into language. Mrs. Pooley's were those good wifely reflections which busied themselves only with her husband's interests, and were disturbed by considerations of what a loss to him the delay would produce should it be further prolonged. Also, there was growing upon her, if it were not already full-grown—as was now the case with all others in the ship—a creepy, indefinable horror of what might be the outcome of this strange affliction that had fallen on the vessel. Suppose, she had asked herself a hundred times in common with all the others on board—the sailors alone expressing their thoughts openly—suppose every- one in the Emperor Succumbed to this blindness! What then would happen, even if it were not followed by death? Would they drift about the ocean helplessly if the calm continued, until they were seen and rescued by some other vessel : or, if a strong gale came up, would they, with no one capable of so much as steering the ship—let alone being able to bend a sail—be shipwrecked and sent to the bottom? While, as to the horrible idea of death following on blindness and the Emperor of the Moon drifting about, floating catacomb—that was not to he thought about I It was too fearful a thing to reflect upon and still preserve one's sanity. Yet, all the same, not only was it thought about but talked about amongst the sailors, but many ideas were propounded as to what was to• be done ere the worst came to the worst. As for Bella, her reflections were all of one kind, and one only. Would Gilbert be spared! For herself she cared but little, though she would scarcely have been the brave, womanly girl she was if she had not repined at the dark cloud which had now settled down over the existence of her lover and herself, and which threatened, if it continued to hover over them and their fortunes, to darken that existence still more. Further than this she did not dare to look, encl., consequently, could only pray fervently that the cloud might be lifted ere long, and strove to force herself to believe that such would un- doubtedly be the case.

Yet Gilbert's meditations were perhaps the most melancholy and bitter of any of the three persons now assembled in the saloon—brave, self-reliant young officer as he was, and full of hope and belief in many happy years still to come and to be passed in the possessioii of a beautiful and devoted wife, as well as in the service of a glorious profession. For ho could not disguise from, nor put away from, his mind the recollection that, with his coming into this ship, with his rescue, there had come also that intangible, mysterious disease which was striking down those around him one by one at extremely short intervals, and, although he knew that he was no more responsible for its presence than had he never been found in that accursed dhow, he began to think that there were many in the Emperor of the Moon who would regard him as more or less so. Which, in truth, was a weak sup- position, born in his usually strong, clear head by the calamities now happening with great frequency one after the other; a supposition shared by no one else in the ship. For—as he himself knew very well, yet took no comfort in knowing—had he not been in the dhow, all the same her other inhabi- tants would have been rescued and taken off by Pooley and have brought on board with them the infection which was now supposed to be at the bottom of the disasters that were happening.

The meditations of all three were now, however, disturbed by the descent of Stephen Charke to the saloon, he being about, to eat his evening meal before taking the first watch. As usual and, almost, it seemed, unjustly soz--since never had he said any further words to Bella which she could construe into an approach to anything dealing with his regard for her—his appearance was disagreeable to her. He seemed, however, to be entirely oblivious of what her sentiments towards him might be, and, after giving a slight bow to both ladies, rang the bell for the steward to bring him his supper. Then, as he seated himself at the table, he said.:

"I fancy we shall have to avail ourselves of your offer of service after all, Lieutenant Bampfyl,3_, and in spite of our having refused it an hour ago. Fagg," he went on, as he cut himself a crust from the loaf, "is attacked with blindness now." "Great havens!" exclaimed Gilbert, while Bella, scarcely knowing why, burst into tears and hid her head on Mrs. Pooley's ample shoulder. "Yes, it is too awful. Also Payn, the bo'sun."

"My God!" And now Mrs. Pooley's fortitude gave way too, and she sobbed quietly to herself until, recognising that two tearful women were scarcely in their proper place in the saloon with these two young men, she rose and, taking Bella with her, they went off to their cabins.

"The watch, of course," went on Charke, "is nothing now with the ship at a standstill. Yet one has to keep it more or less. Fagg's turn would have been the mittdle one to-night, but if you like to fall in you can,take the first, and I'll-" "Thank you," said Gilbert quietly, "but I have done plenty of watch-keeping, bah before and after I was a flag lieutenant. The middle watch won't hurt me. I will relieve you at midnight.."

"As you like. Of course, ihe skipper -and I recognise that it is a great obligation on your part-" "Oh, rubbish! We are absolutely and literally all in the same boat' now, and we've got to make the best of it." Then Gilbert rose and said: "Dy the way, I should like to go and see that poor chap, Fagg, if he is in his cabin. He's a nice young fellow." "He is, and a good sailor, tholigh he doesn't rnake any fuss. Lord knows what's going to be the end of it all. I hope to Heaven, those who are struck won't go the way of those 'niggers; also, that their sight will come back before long." "I should hope so, too; or .else this will be one of the most awful calamities that ever fell upon any ship on a voyage. And the worst is, no one knows what the end is to be." Then he turned on his heel and moved away with the intention of going to

ragg's mum, unite unarte, who was now nen , way through his supper, went on steadily with it yet, as Gilbert reached the gangway outside; the other made afu er re "By th be,' „ other strange thing has happ . -., That-infer-nal tiger-cub of Miss c ' Waldirelh' '' w. her pet!—:Seems'going the same way as the 9thers. It is crawling about the fore-deck in a half-blind fashion, and evidently can't see signs made:before its eyes. As far as the little beast goes\ I shouldn't mind seeing it fall through one of.the scuppers back into.,the sea it was dragged out of. It was rather rubbish to save it at all! , The words "that infernal tiger-cub of Miss Waldron's," grated somehow on Gilbert's feelings, as did also the brutality of the remark about its falling into the sea. Why this was so he did not know, unless it was that he had seen the interest Bella took in the little creature, and in'feeding it and calling everyone's attention to the extraor- dinary manner in which it seemed to grow almost hourly. Nevertheless, the observation did grate on him, arehhe began to tell hi4self that he did not care much for Stephen Charke. However, like a good many other young naval officers, he had thoroughly learnt the excellent system of controll- ing his thoughts in silence, wherefore, without making any further remark than saying that he was sorry to hear about "Bengalee," he went on his way towards Mr. Fagg's cabin, leaving the first mate to finish his supper by himself. He left him, also, to some strange meditatioti which, had they been uttered aloud in the presence of any listener, might have caused that person to imagine that he was the recipient of the babblings of a visionary. Put into words those musings would have taken-some such form as this.

"Supposing this malady or pestilence, or what- ever it is, should be followed by madness and death, as was the case with the negroes. And, supposing also, that, among those who are struck, our friend, Lieutenant Bampfyl&—the future Lord D'Abernoni—should be one. What happens? Bella "—for so he dared to call her in his thoughts and to himself—" Bella is deprived of him. Sup- pose, also, 'that the whole management of the ship falls into my hands; Pooley may be attacked, too —then—then—then—" But, here, his mental ramblings had to come to a conclusion because, wild as his riotous thoughts were, his mind was clear enough to perceive, that he was just as likely to be attacked by the, blindness as were either' Pooley or Bampfyld. Also, he saw very plainly that so, too, was Bella. 'And this pulled his medi- tations up with a jerk, for he could imagine nothing more horrible that could occur now than that the majority of all the men on board should remain sound and unstricken, and capable of working the ;Emperor of the Moon safely into some port or other, while the beautiful girl whom he worshipped and adored so much should succumb to the hateful affliction.

"Oh, my God!" he almost moaned aloud, "if— if she should be the next. If she should be taken and we left. How—how could I endure that ? " And then, because he was a man with the best of impulses beneath all the gall which had arisen in his heart at losing the girl he had once hoped so much to win, he moaned once more: "Not that— not that. Spare her, God, at least! Spare her, even though I have to stand by and see him win her after all. Spare her! Spare her I "

div.head: CHAPTER XIV. STRUCK DOWN.
div.p: CHAPTER XIV. STRUCK DOWN.

But still the days went on and no wind came—the one thing which, even now after they had been becalmed for nearly a week, might have saved the ship from any fearful calamity that was at last, almost without a doubt, in store for her. For, ac- cording to their reckonings, taken regularly both by aid of the brilliant sun which still poured down its vertical rays upon them, and also by the use of a cherub log which they, possessed, as well as the ordinary ones, the current had drifted them some three hundred miles north, so that they had con- sequently the northern coast of Madagascar on their port bow, as well as Tommalin Island, and with Gallga, Providence and Farquhar Islands almost directly ahead of them. Only—the wind would not come, and the ship lay upon the water as motionless, except for the current, as though she had been fixed upon the solid and firm-set earth. And meanwhile the blindness which had seized upon one man after another was still continuing its progress, and more than half— indeed, three-parts of the complement of the Emperor of the Moon were now sightless. Of seventeen sailors, eleven were down with this terrible, paralysing affliction, as well as one officer, Mr. Fagg; so that, if now the long- hoped-for breeze should spring up, there were scarcely enough men in the whole Vessel to set the sails, even including Pooley— who certainly could not go aloft with safety!—and Charke and Gilbert; while, presuming all of them could do so and the wind should freshen,, they would un- doubtedly be far from able to take them in again. And then the result must be swift—undoubted— deadly. The ship would rush to her destruction, be beyond all control; she would either go over under the force of the elements, or be dashed to pieces on some solitary coral island which she might encounter in her mad, ungovernable flight. Con- sequently, there remained bs,„one chance- and one only, for her, that chance ling to forego the advantage of the wind when it came at last, and to let her drift under bare poles until they were seen, and perhaps rescued, -.4 a passing vessel. Only, again arose the fear in all hearts, as already it had done before—would any other ship which might encounter them be willing to take on board men in such a plight as they were, and suffering from a disease that none could 'venture to doubt must be contagious? . Meantime, the life in the vessel itself was, possibly, the strangest form of existence which has prevailed for many a long day in any stout, well-found ship making a- long sea voyage. For she was subject to no stress whatever of weather, the elements were all in favour of her safety, if not her progress; she was comfortable and easy and well found with everything of the best—since in the Emperor of the Moon there was neither rotten pork nor weevily biscuits for old shellbacks to grumble and curse at and mutiny over, as those who wish to make the sailor dissatisfied with his lot are too often fond of representing to be the case—everyone was well housed and well provided with good, wholesome food. Yet, all the same, she was a stricken ship— stricken, in truth, by the visitation of God ; smitten by the hand of God with a curse which none could understand or explain. Fortunately, however—if the word Fortune may be used in connection with those now in her!—this curse seemed to have stopped at the blindness—though Goa knows that was bad enough! Death did not seem to be follow- ing after it, nor madness, nor delirium, as had been the case with the others—certainly as death had been. Those who were d0..-ai '.147 in their berths blind, it is true; but otherwise there was naught else the matter with them; and since they were ministered' to by those who, up to now, had them- selves escaped the visitation, they did not suffer in any other way. Bella and Mrs. Pooley were at this time more or less in charge of the provisions, the latter dealing out the men'S rations under the orders of her husband, while Bella, arrayed in a long white apron which gave her a charmingly strange appear- ance in the eyes of all who beheld her, attended tc the meals of those who used the saloon, took her place in the cook's galley—the unfortunate man being one who was down with the scourge—and saw to all preparations necessary for their now hastily devised and uncomfortable meals. "She's a good'un I" the six remaining healthy MIA mutirvl themselvm, as they saw her busy- ing herself about the ship, making soup and broth for them as well as for the after cabin, and working lindefatigably from morning to night on behalf of all on board, "a real good'un. And this here navy lieutenant what's to marry her is a lord, ain't he, Bill ? " .

"He ain't a lord yet, but he's a-going to be. Ah! well; if we ever all gets safe into oort, her ladyship will know summat about what her ervaliA's ought to be like. Her cooks won't get to windwisrd of her in a hurry, I'll go bail!" "If we ever get safely into port!" That was the sentiment which pervaded ail minds on board the Emperor of the Moon at that time. "If they ever got safely into port!" For all on board now begal to doubt whether they would do so. The eighth day of their being becalmed had come now, even as those forecastle hands discussed the girl's goodness— with also, in whispers, many an admiring remark on her beauty and generally trim built appearance --,the eighth day had come and, suddenly, just as the forenoon watch was over, two more men sud- denly called out together that they were "struck* —were blind! Two more, leaving now only four sailors and three officers—counting Gilbert in place of Fag—and two helpless women! • "Well," said the chief mate, coming up to where Gilbert and Bella were discussing gravely this new affliction, while close by them was going on the usual business of getting the two fresh cases into their berths in the forecastle—which was now a lazaretto—"well, this ends it. The wind way Wow
as much as it Imes now, we anall never Oe sole 10

inake sail. We must drift about till we are picked up or-" Then. seeing the look of terror on Bella's face, he refrainel from flnishing his sen- tence, saying instead: "If we had as many hands to do one man's work as you have in her Majesty's service, Lieutenant Bampfyld, we should still be all right." - • "I don't know," Gilbert replied coldly, and in manner Which, quite unknown to himself, he had been gradually adopting of late towards his unsus- pected, would-be rival. "I don't know. We may have a dozen hands to do one man's work in our Service, as you seem to suggest, and as is often sup- posed, yet, all the genie, I'd back four of our men and two young officers to get a lot of sail on a ship of this size, anyhow." "They might. Yet, clever as they are, your wouldn t like to back them for much to furl those sails again if the breeze freshened into a strong. wind, would you?"
"I think to," said Gilbert, still more coldly. '4At any rate, I'd back them to have a rare good try:"

-"Try!" exclaimed Charke. "T 7 ' Oh, we can all try. As far as that goes, I'd have all the blind ones out to put their weight on the braces while the rest went aloft, if the wind would only come; they could do that without seeing. Also, we could t 7 getting the sails off again if it blew too hard— but I doubt our doing it. Anyone can try." After which he walked forward to make inquiries about the two fre§hTases of blindness. "I don't like that inan, BeIla," Gilbert said when he was out of hearing, "although he's a smart officer and a gentleman. Also, I don't think itk likes me." • -Yor a moment she stood there saying nothing, beifeyes cast down on the soft pitch of the seams, dilichivras greasy and seething under the fierce sun. Then ia he looked up at her lover and said: "No more do I; Bertie, much. In fact, I almost fear him."

"I wonder if -,he was ever in love with you?" Bampfyld said, remembering, as she spoke, how once, in those delicious days when they had first acknow— ledged their own love for one another, she had jokinily told hi-m that he was not the first sailor who had.tried to woo her. Also, he recalled the fact that Charke had been taken to her mother's
house by her uncle, and had been more or less of a frequent Visitor there. "Was he, Bella?" he continued. "Was he the sailor you once told me of, who wanted your love ? "

"Yes," she said, gazing up at him with her clear, truthful eyes, "He was. He told me so long after I met you. And I believe now— I have thought so for some time—that he would never have applied for the position he holds in this ship if uncle hadn't told him that I was coming in it. He was far too ambitious for such a post when I first knew him, and aspired to be captain in one of the great liners, and eventually to be an owner."

"I'm glad you've told me, darling. Especially as, it quite explains his not liking me over much. Poor chap! I can understand that he should not do so in the circumstances," he added, gazing down on his sweetheart with such a glowing look of love as te cause her to forget all their unfortunate sur- roundings and revel only in her delight at being so much beloved by him. "Yet," Gilbert continued, "I can't understand his wanting to come into this ship, even though it would give him three or four months more of your society. Such a thing as that would have been maddening to ordinary men—l know it would have been to me! If you had rejected me—l—l—well, there, I can't say what I should have done; but at any rate, I couldn't have borne the torture of being in your presence—especially if you were on your way to marry another fellow." "He is a strange man," Bella said, "and, although I never loved him, not the least littia- bit, 'I cannot help admiring his force of character. His father, a selfish old man, treated him badly, and baulked him of going into your Service, yet he managed to be a sailor in another way, and to t enforce respect from everyone. Also, he is aT cultivated man and wonderfully well read. Still, I don't altogether like his force of character, or rather, the direction. it takes. He told me onoe,

the day at Portsmouth, that he never faltered in his purpose, and that when once he had made up his mind to do a thing or get a thing he did it, or got it, somehow. I believe, too, that he .meant it as a kind of 4eflance to me." "Did he, iliough " exclaimed Gilbert, as now they sat beneath the awning, at which they had arrived while talking. "Did he! Well, he won't get you, anyway, will he? Not while I'm alive, anyhow. If, however, I were to die-" But this remark was promptly hushed by Bella, who would not allow her lover to even finish it, . _

and, as his watch commenced at six o'clock, he now went below to get an hour or so's rest before that time arrived, while she still sat on beneath the awning, thinking dreamily of him alone and of their future—if any lay before them, which now seemed doubtful or, at least very uncertain.

Then, suddenly, as thus she mused, there happened a thing which startled her, amazed her, so that she sprang out of her Singapore chair and ~..onzed aft. away down towards the south. A thing which even she, a landswoman, a girl originally unacquainted with all connected with seafaring matteri, had, by now, come to recognise and understand as vital to all on board that ship. She had felt the back of the straw • hat she wore(lifted by a slight warm ripple of air, also some ef-the pages of a book she had left lying on the table were suddenly turned over swiftly and with a loud rustle. "It is the Freeze," she 'muttered, "the breeze! The wind atlastl"

The others on deck had perceived it as quickly as she. At once those who were about had sprung into action and thrown off the listlessness which had pervaded all in the ship since they had been becahhed. In an instant all was bustle and con- fusion, the four remaining men who could see moving eagerly. The master came out from where, he had been talking to some of the sufferers, while Charke, running along the waist, called out: "Miss Waldron! Miss Waldron! where is tie lieutenant? We want his services now, at once. Perhaps he, too, can do as much as any of his own men if we look alive."

"I will fetch him directly," she cried, full of, excitement, and swiftly she ran down the com- panion to the saloon on her way to hammer on Gilbert's cabin-door and awaken him. But, as she reached the saloon she stopped, petrified almost.

and filled with a vague alarm at, she scarcely knew what, while, at the same time, she smothered a shriek which rose to her lips, exclaiming in its place: "Bertie I Bertie I What is the matter?" For she saw him standing by the saloon-table gazing at her, smiling even as he heard her loved voice, yet holding on to the edge with one hand while with the other he felt, as it seemed,
cautiously before him. And again she cried: "Bertie, _what is it? What does it mean? "
Then she heard his voice saying: "It means, darling, that I too am struck down. That I too am blind," (To be continued.)

He was conveyed to the Infir- mary.—Edward Miller, 8 years of age, living at 33; Gladstone-street, was knocked down on Twoclay while playing with some other boys, and broke his thigh. div.head: TfiE EXAMINER, FAIDAY, MAX 26, 1899. GENERAL NEWS. I
div.p: TfiE EXAMINER, FAIDAY, MAX 26, 1899. GENERAL NEWS. I

The Q seen celebrat. I her 83th birthday on Viredne;day. Viscount usher, the late Aaster of the Rolls. died on Wed- nesday, The ' Daily Telegraph" nf Wednesday announced the dis- continuance of its Sunday edition. A Germsn h inyeated a beer tablat. You can put One of them in water and it furnishes a good glass of beer.
Henry Carew Cox solicitor, was remanded in custody at Saffron Waidon oa bloaday, charged wit § for ging two deeds.

A great lock-out of all industries connected with the iron and building trade of Denmark began on Wednesd,y all over the country. The trawler Bonito arrivel at Yarmouth on Friday night and reported that three of her crew had been drowned in the North Sea.

Miss Eva Irwin, daughter of a merchant. has died at Belfast fro‘n injuries received 13) collision with a jaunting car while cycling. Mary Bleasdale, a farmer's widow, residing near Colne. has died from injuries iuflictdd by two cows which she was turning out of a field. The annual sale of the Prince of Wales's hackneys teok place at Wolferton on Wednesday. There were 67 horses sold, and they realised 11,601 guineas.
Twelve work men have been killed at Crefeld, Prussia, by the 0011ap3e of the wall of a house on the construction of which they were engaged.

The journal " Rosseva " publishes a telegram from Odessa reporting that Don Jaime. son of Don Carlos, won 200.030 roubles in a lottery on the 13th inst. A monument to the late President Carnot was unveiled at Dijon by President LoubA, who was ae3ompanled by the Premier (M. Dupuy) and other members of the Cabinet.

On Monday two boys named Joosph Pickles and Frederick Laverick, eight years of age, were washed into the sea from the acaham Harbour Pier, and the former was drowned. A collier named James Gibson was reminded at Leigh on MondAy on the charge of causing the deith o another collier named Samuel Henry, in the course of a fight on Saturday, evening.

A gentleman from Richmond was decapitated on Wednes - dty at Charing Cross Station of the Underg mind rtailway through alighting from the wrong door of a carriage and falling under a train. Seven workmen were killed on the spot and three others injured by an explosion which occurred on Wednesday morn- ing at the liilitary Laboratory at Copenhagen. The building wat completely destroyed

Consequent on the 'damage caused by excursionists and numerous accidents during toe ho iday season, Lord Stanley of Alledey has decided ta .;lode the well-known copper mines and adjaeent grounds on Alderley Edge. Mr. Chamberlain, in a letter to Colonel Pryce Jones, M.P., on the subject of the Workmen's Compensation Act, refers to it as the most beneficial to the working classes ever proposed or carried since the grant of free eduJation. A duel has been fought at Ch‘pultepec, Mexico, lotstweln two students of the National Military Academy there. The weapons used were swords, and one student had his heart pierced by a thrust. The other fie I but has been captured. On Tuesday a locomotive engine and a set of trucks, loaded with steel plates and angles, dashed down a declivity at the shipbuilding yard of Mes rs. 11 Iwthorn Leslie and Co., and were lost in the Tyne immediately opposite W allsend.

At Dumtries,Thonaas Camden 3l'Lelland.son of a Wigtown- shire farmer, was oharged with murdering his aunt. It is alleged that the prisoner wrished 13,r to sign two bills for £1,030, and upon her rellisiag shot her fatally with a revolver.

An explosion of firedamp occurred on Monday morning at the Benarty pit of the Lochore and Capeldrae Cannel Coal Company, Fifeshlre. Three men were at work repair- ing roads at the time, and Joseph Harail'xin, forty-four, was killed outright. A duel with sabres was fought on Saturday at Madrid be - tween two majors of the Army of Cuba. One of them had been a member of the Tribunal of Honour,which had inquired into the conduct of the other oflizer. One of the duellists was wounded.

According to a telegram to the "Post," frorn Warsaw, the town of Poroson,in the Government of Grolno,has been com- pletely destroyed by fire. Twelve lives were lost, while about 3 000 persons were rendered homeless,and are camping out in the fields.

Madame Sarah Bernhardt appeareclas Hamlet on SaturdaY night, at her theatre in Paris and achieved a great success. She presented the appearance of a very youthful Hamlet, her acting was very fine throughout, and she was repeatedly called be!ore the curtain.

Two terrible fatal ferry boat accidents are reported from Bavaria. At Hoermannsdorf, a Danube ferryboat capsized owing to the breaking of the rope, and fourteen of the passen- gers were drowned; and at Simbavh a boat capsized on the Inn, ten persons losing their lives. The death is announced of the negro Isaac Phillips, who was stabbed at Hartlepool recently by his landlord, also a negro, named Thomas Thompson, who fatally shot his wife on the same occasion. A coroner's jury returned a verdict of " Wilful murder" against Thompson. A raven has been known to live sixty-nine years ; a pair of eagle owls lived sixty-eight and the ot',er fifty-three years ; a Bateleur eagle and a condor in the Zoological Gardens, at Amsterdam, fifty-five and fifty-two years ; an imperial eagle fifty-six, a golden eagle forty-six, and a sea ea.gle forty-two years. _

Presiding on Monday at the opening, at Brighton, of the forty-fourth session of the Sona of remp.rance, Bro. E. Hallswot th said they had a membership of 42,775 adults and 18,333 juvenile., with accumulated funds £193,251 4s, and 954 subordinate divisions and cadet sections in thirty-six grand divisions. On Wednes .ay, during a heavy thunderstorm which passed over North Notts, the lightning struck Welbeck Abbey, the seat ot the Duke of Portland. The whole of the leadwork was ripped away from the turret clock, an I many of the squares of glass in the windows of the grand dint ng roam were smashsd.

Two Norwegian sailors, named Albin Petersen and Oakar Sjoback. are in custody at Gloucester on a charge of murder- ing a fellow-conntryman named Andrew Andersen, who, on arrival of the midnight mail from Milord Haven, wts found dead in a carriage with a terrible stab in the neck. ..,joback's purse was found on the deceased. While a party of four Salvationists were trying to get from the top of Lteachy Head to the shore, one of them slipped and fell a distance of 100 feet. sustaining fatal injuries. Two of the party succeeded in returning to the summit, and the other held on some 43 feet down until the cosstguards, with very great difficulty, managed to effect a rescue. A telegram from Vancouver. British Columbia, reports that Dawson City was almost totally destroyed by fire on the asth April* One hundred and eleven buildings in the business part of the city have disappeared. Two banks were burned oat. and a large amount of money, estimated at one million dollars, destrayed. The total loss in property, sc., is es- timated at several millions. There were no casualties.

On Sunday. Alice Higginbotham. ten years old, slipped and sell whilst gathering wild flowers on the top of Lovers' Leap, Buxton. Dan feet down she was caught by a tree and a ledge, and in that awful position she lay still as death until the fire ecspe was fetched and reseued her. She was not hurt. Had she moved she would have fallen forty feet. During the Whitsuntide fair at Preston. George Slater, aged 53, engine tE,uder. of Skeffington-road, Prestoa,went on the steam roundabouts. Just as the machine was slowing. Slater, who was accompanied 'l,sf his wife and child, aged seven, fell off, alighting on the back of his head. He was picked up unconscious and removed to the infirmary, where he died shortly after his admission.

livery sailor is aware of the absolute impossibility of ex- cluding rats from a ship. They seem, however, to have a special liking for the modern battleship. It is not long since the Oollingwood had to be sent to Devonport in order that the rats might ibe removed frona her, and now it is the Devastation, at Gibraltar which is infested. It is said that in this case the rats have become so bold that they will even bite the Ballot $ in their hammocks.

A startling shipping disaster, though, fortunately, involv- ing no sacrifice of life, occurred on Sunday morning, the American liner Paris, from Southampton and Cherbourg for New Yolk, ruaning ashore on the Manacles, off the oast of Cornwall. The vessel had on board 380 passengers, who were all landed in safety, the sea being relatively calm. The balance of testimony points t 3 the fact that there WO no fog, but only a drizzling rain. The Paris has been lightened of her cargo, but still remains on the rocks. A shocking lynching outrage is reported:from, Diaz, State of Chihuahua, Mexico. One Spanish negro, who had at temptel to assault the wife of a rmich-awuer. was tracked by blo3dhounds. Nine other uegroes found at the plaee where the man was run down, but who scorn to have had no connection with the assault, were also captured, and of the ten three were hung and four others shot when attempting to :cape. A rat's tail is a wonderful thing. The great naturalist envier says that there are more muscles in this curious appendage than are to be found In that part of the human anatomy whkh is most admired for its ingenious structure— namely, the hang. To the rat, in fact, its tail serves as a sort ot hand, by means of which the animal is enabled to crawl along ledges or other difficult plasages, using it to balance with or to gain a hold. It is prehensile, like the tails of some monkeys. By means of it the little beast can jump up heights otherwise inaccessible, employing it as,a projective spring.

A-,. " Morn-ing Levier" telegram, dated New York, Tuesday says :—The outcome of the war race in Bast :New York, the Whitechapel of this city, between Americans and immigrants was the branding. yesterday. of a child of tour of foreign parents, who are unable to speak English. Three men branded him on the hip with the word Chicsgo, by means of a heated 51n die, the result being an atrocious wound. William Masterton, a blacksmith. will was -concerned, has been arrested. The foreign immigrants are hated because they work cheaper, and thug oust Americans.

The consumptionof horseflesh is growing in Paris tl such an extent that it is proposed to erect a special abattoir for the hippophagists. At present the slaughtering of horses for human food is carried on at Villejuif, and last year 15,137 animals. including 257 donkeys were consumed. The meat welghed3343 700 kilos. The consurnptiou of horseflesh is. of course, no now thing in Prance. The first horse sisughte - house was opened in 1866. Hippophagist s claim that horse- flesh Is better and as nourishing as that of any other animal. The obvious objection is that the animals killed in Paris are generally old, worn-out basks or horses which meet with accidents.

div.head: MESSRS. RICHMOND'S
div.p: MESSRS. RICHMOND'S
PRO-kit SHARLIG SCI-IEIIIE.

The annual profit sharing distribution in connec- tion with Messrs. Richmond and Co., Limited, gas app iratus manufacturers, of Warrington, Stratford and London, to3k place in one of the workrooms in Academy-St., Warrington,on Friday afternoon. Mr. E. W. T. Richmond (chairman of the com- pany and managing director) presided, and he was supported on the platform by Mr. H. es. Ransoms (director and Warrington manager), Mr. H. M. Thornton (director and Stratford manager), Mr. L. Voisey(secretary to toe clmpany), Mr. H.P. Hughes (hon secretary to' the Profit-Sharing Committee) Mr. J. Pollitt, Mr. Davy (works manager) Mr. C• R. Adamson, Mr. S. A. Scrivener,and Mr. J. A. Ran- sume (representatives) Some hundreds of work- men were present. The CHAIRMAN, who was received with rounds of applause on rising to speak, said he was sorry that his throat was so bad that he was unable to speak to them. He had, however, written some- thing of What he intended to say, and he would ask Mr. Ransome to read it. (Applause). Mr. RANsomis then read the notes of Mr. Rich- mond, which were ai follow

"I regret excesdingly that I am physically incap- able of addressing you to-day. It is only the import- ance that I attach to the profit sharing which has brought me to Warrington to-day. I feel, however, that although I cannot actually speak to you, yet ehould like to have a message read to you which will embody some of the matters upon which 1 should have been glad to have addressed you. (Applause.) 111 the first place you will be interested to know that the amount of money we are to distribute to-.lay is £746 ald this is considerably more than we distributed on the last occasion. (Applause.) The individual amounts are also heavier as there is al2 months prufit sharing against a previous six months. Some of our employees amongst the men are receiving up to £5 or a and some of our boys as much as 153 and £l. One thing that greatly exercises my mind in connection with teis matter is the desire that those of you who have not taken the whole of your bonus in shares will take great care of the cash portion and let it form a nest egg to which you may aid such sav- ings as you can effect, week by week. (Applause.) Depend upon it, the habit of saving grows up on you and if you only commence to save a little, no matter how small, you will find that as you grow accustomed to saving, you will increase the amount you put by until in the course of a few years, you will be surprised how much you are able to save, and what a spien lid total the savings have amounted to. The fact that this money we are distiibutine to-thy is sm. thing over and above wages, and something which comes entirely out ot the company's profits, points very definitely to the fact that we as a company ought te benefit by this extra outlay. We feel that the money we are giving to- day, and the shares, are rutting it within the p senor of every man to improve his position in life, and we think you will feel that your part is to return this in the same spirit, and do your best for the company, by preventing waste. If you can see cheaper ways of producing goods point them out to your foreman. Don't be afraid of do- ing a good day's work for a good day's pay.' (Applause). You will remember on the last occasion that I addressed you on this subject ,Mr. George Livesey, of the South Metropolitan Gas Company presided at our meeting held on the South side of the works, and in the course of his well thought out speech he told you that labour had its place,and capital had its place,and that without brains and capital, and the enterprise which goes to make a business, labour would be without employment, and that you must not run away with the idea that labour alone was to be considered in the distribution of the profits. I am exceedingly sorry to say that since our last meeting Mr. Frank Livesey, one of the pioneers of profit sharing, had passed away, and by his death the working-classes of this country has lost a most valuable friend. As we are aware, this profit sharing ex- tends right from our representatives who being in the businees which keeps us all employed, down through our office staff, and right through every department of our works. (Applause ) In conclu€ion let me,on behalf of my e-o Directors and myself,express my earnest desire that your lives may be bright and prosperous and that we may work together with a hearty goodwill and continue to expand in the future as we have done in the past. (Applause.) Mr. RANSOMN (continuing) said he was sue they would agree with him that if Mr. Richmond's voice had been in better condition and had enabled him to speak they would have had a very much more eloquent speeeen and perhaps have gained a good deal riFre information from it. This subject of profit 84 g was one of growing interest to the men. Many of the nyn had already got four or five shares in the company and that number would be increased after the present distribution. As their shaqs increased, the men would feel tbe benefit of them. (Bear, hear.) When the profit-sharing scheme was started many men were inclined to scoff at it, but as their savings increased from pounds to tens of pounds and hundreds of pounds —if they only lived long enough—(laughter)--he be- lieved they would feel that they bad something sub- stantial to fall back upon on a rainy day. (Bear. hear.) The shares which they had taken up were as good as cash. If they were leaving through sickness or special causes they could realise the amount of money the shares represented, although from the company s'andpoint that. was not the object for which the shares were riven. The idea was that the men would look forward with in- terest to the dividend they were to receive from the shares they held in the company. Be thought they had reason to be thankful to Mr. Richmond for the able way he had brought this profit-sharing about. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He did not know of another foundry or a company like theirs in the United King- dom. or even in the world, where there was such a system of profit-sharing, and he believed they had got the eyes of the industrial world upon them, seeing if Richmond's profit-sharing was a suw:ess. He felt that a great deal depended upon the men them- selves; they could make it a success or they could mar it. It would be ungracious on their part, if, after the energetic way Mr. Richmond had worked to brine it about, they were to do anything to mar 'it in any way. He hoped every man would have the profit sharing scheme very much at heart. (Hear, hear.) There had been many inquiries made by various com- panies as to how the scheme worked. He was glad to say that they had been able to give a satisfactory reply. (Applause.) He would not like to say that there was notia man uncontented. He dare say they had heardrof men who had left them but who still desired to hold ' their shares. The committee decided that that could not be se, and it was rather a compliment to the men who held shares that those outside would like to have them if they ceuld. (Hear, hear.) They could not do less than pass a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Riohmond for being present that day, seeing that under the cir- stances Mr. Richmond ought to be in bed or at least at home. It showed what a generous spirit they had got at the bead of the firm when he would rather be amongst his own men than at home being cuddled up in an arm chair. (Laughter.) He would now ask Mr. Thornton. the manager of the Stratford Works, to second the vote of thanks. It was very gratifying that such a cordial feeling existed between the two works. He was sure all present would wish to convey to the Stratford men their hearty good wishes: (Applause.) Mr. THORNTON in seconding the vote of thanks, said he was sure they all regretted Mr. Rich- mond's inability to address them, but they had had an able substitute in Mr. Ransoms. (Hear, bear.) He hoped Mr. RAll,9oftle had completely recovered from his illness, and that they would not have to send him to Egypt again. (Laughter). Referring to the working of the profit-sharing scheme at Stratford, Mr. Thornton said he remarked to one of the workmen that his bank- ing account was getting on, all he replied," It is not SO dusty " (Laughter). In looking through their cata- logue of goods, be thought Mr. Richmond must have had some idea of his own future, when he named some of their productions. There was for instance the " Mansion House" cooker, and that was adopted before Mr. Richmond had any thought of going to Lan- don. (Laughter) Then again in adopting the names " Richmond "and "Gordon," he must have had an eye to the title of the Dnkc of Richmond and Gordon (Laughter.) Some of the-4;nes might also be applied to the profit-sliarin,9: scheme: It was now as plain to them its" A B C." (Laughter.)Fle daresay it was not so easy at first but it was now. This was largely due to the energy of their secretary, Mr. Hughes. (Applause) A e entleman who had been looking into the scheme said he had never seen such a splendid arrangement of profit- sharing before. He thought a great deal of credit was due to Mr. Huehes, who, as Mr. Ricbmord reminded him,had spent a great deal of time and labour on it. Lt them hope that it might be a model for other companies to cony. (Hear, hear.) He was sure they hoped it would be "universal;" that it would become "national;' and that Mr. Richmond would now hand them the "Royal Sovereigns.-' (Laughter and applause.) Mr. E. W. T. RICHMOND then made the distribu'ien to the employes. Ho afterwards thanked them for their kind vote of thanks and mentioned the receipt of a tele- gram from Mr. W. Atkins of Malvern. Director, and one from Mr. C B Vessey of Sheffield, Direci-or, in -wllieh they expressed their best wishes and regretted that they were unable to be present at the meeting.

process of getting ready for the departure occupied about an hour. At six o'clock tee men marched to the lawn in front of the Town Hall, where they were formed into companies and the roll called. Two Volunteers who had imbibed to freely were ordered off the field, and left to repent 'Of their foolishness. The spectators, whose numbers had rapidly increased, and who were at first eotatent to view the proceedings from the paths round the grass plot, now crowded as close to the men as possible, and the result was afterwards seen in no little damage being done to the lawn. The regi- mental band, under the direction of baquiaster Thomas Armstrong, was in attendance, and wten the signal was given for the departure for Bank Quay Station, it struck up a well-known , air, fol- lowed by "Auld Lang Syne." The men pre'sinted a smart and soldierly appearance as they proceeded to the station. They quickly entrained, and at 6-40 the special steamed out of the station amidst cheers.

Conway was reached at 10.5 p.m. in darkness but fortunately the weather was dry. Everything was found in readiness for them, and, notwithstanding the heavy rains of the previous three daS7s, all the beds were as dry as if the sun had been shining brightly througoout the week, and this happy state of things was owing to the excellent arrangements which nad been made by Captain and Quartermaser T Hutchinson, and his able coadjutor, Quarter- master-sergeant A. F. G. Potter. These gentlemen are also in charge of the commissariat department, which is being well looked after,the meat,vegetattles and bread supplied to the men from day to day being all one could desire. A good staff of cooks has been requisitioned, and the meals—bre ilrfast, dinner, and tea—are served with punctuality. The total strength of the Warrington corps early in the week was 19 officers, 44 sergeants, 12 buglers, and 342 rank and file ; total 417. The officers in cams are Colonel J C Ridgway (commanding), Major II .1 Widdowes, Major J D Buckton, Captains R W Baynes, J A Edelsten,F M Appleton.J D Fairclough, J El Ridgway, B Feirclough ; Lientenants G R Oros- field, 1E Bernhard, E G Medley, C F Carey, E F Willcocks, C P Gough; Captain and Adjutant F M Roo tne,Captain an I Quartermaster Thomas Hut ch in son, Surgeon-Captain Adams, and Surgeon-Lieu- tenant J M Patterson. The Rector also stayed two or three days in camp. The transport section is in charge of Lieutenant Crosfield and Sergeant Connor; Captain Appleton is in charge a the cycling corps; ' Lieutenant Patterson is responsible for the stretcher- bearers section. and NIT.. Thomas iiirmstrong is ati his old post as regimental bandma ter. The bugle band is controlled by Corporal Campbell. An efficient orderly room sergeant is found in the person of Mr. J. T. Bennion. The catering for the officers has been entrusted to Mrs. Barker and Mrs. Powis, and valuable services are also rendered in this connection for the sergeants by Mr. D. Morris, of Wilderspool-road, Warrington. and Mr. Walter Potter, and in each case every satisfaction is being given. • The whole of the Fusiliers came into camp in the course of Sunday, arriving in the order of their position in the Army list.. The brigade, as usual, in command of Major-General W. Thack well, C 8.,' brigadier of the Lancashire Brigade, who has with ; him Lieutenant-Colonel the lion RJ 0 Jocelyn nal brigade-major; Major J D Buckton (let V. 8.) as A.D.C. ; Captain J A Edelsten (Ist V.B.S.L ) as sup-1 ply and transport officer; and Sergeant-Major tialibia (3rd V.8.L.F.) 89 brigade sergeant-major. F Haworth and 26,officers. This bat'alion arrived in camp below its tvual camp strength. This is attributed partly to the bad weather, and partly to a general feeling anatink the men in favour of a change of venue in the matter of camping ground. div.head: LOCAL VOLUNTEERS UNDER CANVAS. UNPLEASANT EXPERIENCES.
div.p: LOCAL VOLUNTEERS UNDER CANVAS. UNPLEASANT EXPERIENCES.

Our local volunteers have this week been experi- encing the pleasures and displeasures of camp life: Whit-week has now become associated with en- campments of the volunteers of Lancashire and Cheshire, but th 3 weather which has been experi- enced in recent years can hardly be said to have justified the selection of this holiday season for such a purpose. Instead of a bright sun, a cloud- less sky and a gentle sea breeze, all of which are necessary to make camp life pleasant and endura- ble, there have been for the past two seasons at least, boisterous gales, accomPanied by heavy rains. A piece of canvas affords but a very ineffective shelter against the inclemencies of the British climate, and Volunteers fresh from their homes are not the best to rough it when the I weather is at its worst. There is this much, how- ever, to be said in favour of Conway that its situa- tion lends itself better for an encampment than Ethyl, where the Warrington volunteers had such an unpleasant experiencs twelvemontlis ago. Des- pite the unfavourable weather this week, the incon- veniences have not been .so great as was the case

last year. The tents which have been provided have been of better quality, and the ground has absorbed the rain more quickly. Then again, instead of occupying an isolated position at !thy!, they have had the company of three other Lancashire battalions, and by smoking concerts and other means pleasant companionships have been made. The number of volunteers in camp shows a diminu- tion upon that of last year, and probably the hard- ships then experienced have had something to do with it. Not quite 400 made the journey on Satur- day, but others have tollowed during the week, and when the inspection takes place to-day, the numbers will probably have increased to 600. The magnificent camping ground formed by the Conway Niorfa is this year occupied by a brigade consisting in the main of former visitors, though numerically inferior to its predecessors. The brig- ade emcamping on this ground has usually con- sisted of eight battalions (although these rarely meet together) under the title of the Cheshire and Lancashire Brigade. It appears, however, to have been found that the ground available for manceuvr- ing such a large body of men (consisting of from 5,000, to 6,000 troops) was too limited, and a re- duction in the number of battalions has this year taken place. With this change in numbers has come ' a change in the title of the brigade, and the four battalions now in camp are described as the Lanca- shire Brigade, which in its entirety is composed of five battalions—namely, -Ist, 2nd, and 3rd V B LF, and the Ist (Warrington). and 2nd (St. Helens) VBS L. Of these five.battalions, however. the St. ' Helens contingent is this year emdamped at Black- p3ol, so that now, for the first time in the history of a brigade camp at"Conway,the whole of the men are red-coated. Last, year,/ considerable dissatisfaction was felt on account of ,the quality of the tents sup- plied to the troap,sonany of them, being, very old, let in water to 'an extent which made camping very uncomfortable, and led to scomplaints, it; cones- quence Of which, RA fitkoector camis.down last year jad condemned, a large number of the tents. This yaar there is a very satisfactory iMprovement in this respect, nearly all, the tents being new, while all of them are of the latest pattern.. Fatigue par- ties have been on the ground since Wednesday of last week,.but the weather has been snbad that -up to Saturday they had to work inoilskins: In spite of the wet weather, they -were able: tnget every-

thing i , - i • - n shipshape order for the arrvalbEthe troops. THE celebrations of Wednes- day, the area over which they Popularity. ranged, the messages received the sentiments uttered, the goodwill expressed, all show that the Sovereign of these realms occupies a position in the world and in the affections of her people at home and abroad which has never been equalled in history. This is a significant fact, and it cannot be challenged, it will not even be doubted. As a Sovereign the QUEEN has reigned for an extraordinariby long period, and:sho is more popular now in her age and her declining years than she was at any previous period of a career especially marked ny many signs of affec - tion and personal respect. Other Sovereigns have made a greater stir, either by reason of their am- bitions, or their misfortunes, but none has lived to bear the burden of so many years of rule, or has seen so many changes in her Ernpire,or has been so near to the hearts of the people. The Victorian era is as distinct in its way as any of the great eras in our history, and it can now be truly said that three of them have been associated with the name of a female Sovereign. The Elizabethan,the Augustan reriod of Queen ANNE, and now the Victorian period have been notable for distinct national features,all contributing to the advance- ment of this country, and to the betterment, the elevation, the prosperity of the people. But neither the VIRGIN Queen nor Queen ANNE was so near to the hearts of the people as has been Queen VICTORIA. There are many reasons for this popularity, and it is worth while referring to some of them. The QUEEN has kept her Court pure,and she has never allowed the breath of scandal to touch her private life. She has been strictly im- partial in her dealings with pclitical parties. She has honoured persons of all grades, religions, and degrees of attainment and merit. In all times of suffering and distress, whether sharp and temporary or national and prolonged, she has been in close sympathy with her people, with the heroes who have done brave deeds in peace or war, in philanthropy, in adventure, or in literature, art, and science. Her domestic life has been attuned to very high ideals. As a mother, a wife, and a widow she has been natural, true, and simple-hearted. Her grief for the Prince Consort though it seemed at one time to be almost morbid in its intensity, has endeared her more than ever, to her people. Of late she has made less and less of the" divinity that doth hedge" a Sovereign Her Journals of the Highlands were a pleasant surprise to many, as revealing the sincerity and simplicity of a genuine womanly nature. The re- ception they had in the country has induced her allow more details to be known of her daily P
ate and official life. We doubt whether as-mue Is known in any country in the world as there'

in this country of the normal daily life and official duties of the Sovereign. It is still necessary ta secure privacy, and to protect the persoa of the Queen from accidents and the eccentricities of madmen and fanatics, the rush of crowds, and the effusive loyalty of the people. But there has never been any conspiracy against her, any grave attacks Upon her in the country or in the press, and the Poorest folk in the land are as ready to say affec- tionate things of the QUEEN as the highest nobles Who attend the Court and rejoice in her friend- ship. We venture to say that this personal popu- larity is as noteworthy as anything connected With our beloved QUEEN, and for many days to - corn° proofs will be as abundant as they will be Pleasant and convincing.

THE Conference will compel The Discussion about us to discuss a number of War. awkaid questions we are constantly disposed to thrust aside as fit only for Professors and political economists. It will do good in this way, if it should not result in chang- ing by magic the tendency of some countries to- wards warlike solutions of international difficul- ties. What, for instance, must be the political and moral effect of organising a whole nation on a military basis? There must be some difference iO temper, in social life, and in political attitude between two countries, one of which is pacifically and the other militarily inclined. But where can we find pacific nations just now ? The purely Pacific nation used to be Great Britain, but it has been caught in the infection, and of late it has been spending millions extra in naval and military armaments. There is no other country, unless it be Holland, and Holland is not In the first rank. Even the -United States of America has caught the war-spirit, and has been interfering in Spanish affairs, at a great expendi- ture of money, with very doubtful results. All the nations are armed or arming, and the nations which ha7e neglected their duty in this respect, such as China and Spain, have gone down before a stronger pwer. Turkey has now come into the Ting of organised Powers, and has reserves and a Mobilisation scheme. Sa far as the events of the last half century teach us any ±ing, they impress on the fact that or,raniza,tion for war hardly lessens its frequency. In fifty years we have had a civil war in America, wars in Italy, in Austria,in France,and In Russia and Tarkey,to say nothing of the Indian Mutiny, the invasion of Afghanistan, Burmah,and Cores, and the rise and fall of Mandism in Africa. It does not appear that peace has come with advancing civilisation, and yet the repose between 1815 and 1850 was almost profound, at any rate in Western Europe. A war period is followed by a Peace period. The present Conference is an attempt to avert another war period, and hence we all wish it success. It is more than that, because it offers a substitute for the arbitrament of arms. -Will it do much, if anything, to avert the political and social disasters which elaborate and costly military systems must entail ? In Germany a Particular type of Sacialism has followed military organisation and military success ; and Socialism is quite consistent with mili- tarism, and if there is to be an organised army of industrialists, all State-paid, why , should there not also oe an army of soldiers, all State-paid? For effective fighting purposes, a socialised Germany might be as strong as a Ger- many on individualist lines. In France we have seen the army becone an object of blind worship, demoralising its officers and the people. In this country we have manifested a disposition to mag- nify skirmishes into battles, and to make heroes of Wounded pipers and Maxim-using colonists. Is war always to have this bad ethical result ? Does it mean,for us,inevitable political deterioration? Is the earth to come to an end in the form of a great Armagddon ? We have got to discuss these 'questions tat now. They are in the air. It willdo Lis good to understand what militarism, Empire, and glory-swagger really means.
now came the Paris on the Manacles? The

9uestion is easily,eagerly asked, but no answer Isforthcorning. Surmise and enquiry alike fail to throw light on the problem, and in the mean- time the great American liner remains on the rocks, a prey to every variation of tide and Weather. Fortunately the win ls have so far been light, and there is a possibility of saving the ves- sel before she becomes a total loss. The pas- sengers were all saved, and since one a-m. on Sunday they have cause for deep thank- fulness to a merciful Providence for the preserva- tion of their lives in one of the most critical sit- uations possible. There has never been any satisfactory explanation of the wreck of the Mobegan within a mile of the spot where the Paris 'lies, and the) plunging of over one hundred souls into eternity is as.. much a mystery
llow as at the time of its. happening.- This

_ catastrophe had begun to fade— from- men's minds, and had become but an unhappy memory, When an even bigger vessel re-aroused the excite- lalebt and re-doehied the mystery by c-iming to grief on the same terrible rocks. The Paris was a full thirty miles out of her proper course from have to New York, and no one appears to nave the slightest idea worth serious consideration as to how she got in these waters. One theory is Fiat the coast, rocky and metallic in formation, magnetic properties which have lured the essel to destruction—a la Sindbad's experience. here may even be something in this _ldea, but we are inclined to doubt it. If the rocks cou'd so affect the course °f vessels pass7ng through the channel, the num- ber of such di casters must of necessity be far greater than it is. No vessel approaching within a cer- tain radius would escape, and there must be scores of instances in which they come finite c;ose to the 'coast without experiencing the ill-fortune of the Mohegan and Paris. There only -teems to be one explanation possible, and that is that someone has blundered, and _ _

blundered 'A wf ull y. We hope that the official en- quiry may solve the mystery. It will not take much more to frighten voyagers into forsaking all I;outes which necessitate the navigation of the `'hannel with its uncanny Manacles.
