----- The seven-day newspapers have had a short :ar.eer, and without exposing wounds it may be iald they have yielded to the force of public opm- -10°,1:1. They were not started on philanthropic w"nciPles, anti it would be hard to credit that they t ere given up on these grounds, though it is easy ° Bee that they could have prolonged the fight

with some uncertainty as to the result. Mr. Smalley, in a review of seven-day journalism in New York which appeared in the" Times," points • out dint the same protests were made in A menc-t ' on their initiation there as were made here a few weeks ago, but from lack of vigour they failed. There has been no lack of vigour on this side. Never had newspapers to meet such a combination of protestors. Roman Catholics rose above their Roman Catholicism, and Dissenters above their Dissent, and linked their names together in united objection to the Sun lay news- paper. Even Lord Halifax and Lord Kinnaird, as representing the two wings of the English Church, were prepared to tolerate the views of the head of their Church, the Arch- bishop of Canterbury, on this subject. Then there was the Labour party, which forgot its differences in this encroachment on its liberties,and the trade the Newsagents' Union, which realised that the extra pence were not worth the taking at the coat of the day's recreation. The main objection to the seven-day newspapers was the humanitarian' that it tended to destroy the day of rest. Mr. John Burns hit oft the situation in a phrase. If seven- day newspapers, why not seven-day insurance canvassing ? And men shuddered when they thought of the army of touts who might descend upon them at their private houses, knowing they would find them snugly at home. The Sunday as a day of rest has done much for the greatness of this country, while Sunday yellow journalism has driven away from America the men who have made their fortunes there. Mr. W. W. Astor has con- firmed this during the present week. The American journals are vulgar, without being funny.

"The Effects of the Factory System" is the title of an interesting work by Mr. Allen Clarke, whose revelations will come as a surprise to many people. We learn that upwards of 100,000 children of tender years are employed as half-timers in Lancashire textile factories, the County Palatine thus being responsible for the employment of at least 57 per cent of the factory half-timers in the country. It has been a theory held for some time in certain quarters that the early attention to factory-life and daily toil imposed on the half- timers, has the effect of sharpening their faculties to such an extent that they easily hold their own with their class-mates at school. But this is not quite the true aspect of the case. "Early familiarity with work" says Mr. Clarke "certainly forces their intelligence up,but like all forced maturity, it soon collapses." The children eventually lose their quickness of perception, become drowsy, and show all the signs of brain-fag. By the time he has reached manhood the half-timer is educationally-handicapPed, stunted in physical growth, and capable of little beyond a mechanical application to his daily work. Parents have some- thing to answer for in this respect. Mr. Clarke is not far wrong when he alleges that "the majority of parents in Lancashire regard children only as commercial speculations, to be turned into wage- earning machines as soon as the child's age and the law permit." They are thus opposed to legisla- tive interference in the condition of t'Aeir children. This attitude of the parent is a serious stumbling- block to the proper administration of elementary education,while it dwarfs to a minimum the child's opportunities for physical and moral development. 'Tis no wonder that one can stand by any factory- yard gate and see emerge a crowd of toil-worn, un- dersized operatives,whose faces are the index of the stagnant nature within. These facts point strongly to the need for legislation in several directions,but it is too much to hope that anything will be done in this branch of social reform while others, such as old-age pensions, and the housing of the work- ing classes, are pressing so strongly for attention.

It is curious that while public opinion got into such a ferment about the publication of seventh- day newspapers, little agitation against other in- fractions of the rule to keep the Sabbath holy is aroused. We are so accustomed to the running of railway trains and omnibuses on Sunday that we seldom stop to consider the religious aspect of this form of Sunday labour, and if we did we should probably be constrained to shelve the question owing to the unanswera.bleness of the argument that trains and omnibuses are necessary for the public convenience on Sunday, as on other days, though to a somewhat less extent. But the opening, in rapidly increasing numbers, of music halls, theatres, assembly rooms, etc., for concerts on Sunday afternoons and evenings ought to at- tract a little more attention than it does. In the metropolis applications have been made to the County Council by no fewer than ten music halls and the like, for permission to open on Sundays for Sunday music, and the license has been granted on an understanding that the concerts shall not be given by way of trade or for private gain. All these applications are in addition to those which were heard at the last licensing sessions of the County Council, so that it is quite plain that the love of this form of entertainment is spreading rapidly. People can enjoy—or ought to be able to enjoy—their day of rest without resorting to the music hall with its attendant odours and un- Sabbatarian surroundings. Sunday music in such places is unnecessary. There is plenty of it to be had at the churches whose doors ever stand open, and wherein there is no suggestion of a perform- ance for pecuniary gain —as there is bound to be in the music hall, the requirements of the law not- withstanding. The English Sunday, even yet, is plainly in some danger of developing into a facsimile of the unholy seventh day of Oa Con- tinent.

WHITSUNTIDE IN RUN- CORN DISTRICT. The observan:es of the Whitsuntide holidays I have been of the usual kind, takinq the form of I Sunday s :hoot demonstratious at Runcorn, and Hal- ton " Miserable holiday weather " has been the cry on all sides—yet, with characteristic stubborn- ness, huudreds of holi lay makers hale been mak- ing the best of their time. They have tied, and not altogether tailed, in getting through a wet Whitsuntide, with the most enjoyment that that such unpropitious climatic conditims would allow. On Monday, the streets of Runcorn presen- ted a wretc)ed appearance, and the school chil- dren's demonstration became an exhibition of umbrellas and overcoats. 80 that keen disspolint- ment was felt at the compulsory covering up of what for years has been Runcorn's gorgeous pagent—" The School Children's Persia." But for s!1 the rain, the children enjoyed what followed in the shape of tea ani cake, at their respective schools.

SUDDEN DRATEI AT ORFORD. The death of James Norman, aged 71 years, of Sandy-lane, Orford, took place on Sunday. The deceased had been ailing for many year, but of late had apparently been in ;pod health. He called to his wife on Sunday, at 11.30 a.m., that he was suffering from an attack of spasms, but he would not allow her to send for Or. White, who was pilis• ing at the time. At nyelve o'clock he had anotaer attack to which he succumbed.

At the monthly meeting of ttie Runcorn Free Library Committee held at the Town Hall on Thursday, there were present:—Messrs W Handley (presiding),E Imison, S Pop., D Bisbrown, M J Sweetman, W J Cunningham, F W Hutton, with J D Jones (librarian). div.head: DEATH OF ME. HUGH_ ROWE, HALTON.
div.p: DEATH OF ME. HUGH_ ROWE, HALTON.

We regret to announce the death of Mr. Eilu!,h Rowe, which took place at Halton, on Saturday afternoon. The deceased had been in ill health for the past eighteen months, and confined to his bed since Christmas. He was one of Hilton's oldest anl most respected i thabit- ants. For 25 years he held office as overseer, and for a similar pericd he was officially connected with the Hal- ton Court Leet. He was, in his better health, an active and zealous member of the Wesleyan body, and for over 50 years was identified with the Sabbath school. In recognition of his long and valuable services to the Sab- bath school movement the Sunday School Union recently presented him with a long service medal. The funeral cook place at Halton on Wednesday afternoon and was largely attended, despLe the heavy downpour of rain Tne deceased's remains were laid to rest in the pretty little cemetery, amidst the visible manifestations of regret of the whole community, and in the loss of Mr. Rowe the village mourns one of its grea'eit m;sfortunes. div.head: FUTURE OF RUNCORN. NEW AVENUES OF EIIPLOYMENT.
div.p: THE FUTURE OF RUNCORN. NEW AVENUES OF EIIPLOYMENT.

There has just seen conciuded in the " Liverpool Weekly Mercury" a series of *ketches concerning Run- corn end district. The ultimate article contains the following passages, which should interest residents and others "Is the trade of Rawson/ declining or reviving ?' Certain pessimistic crit:cs whose alarmist views serve no better purpose than those of creating a feeling of apprehension whin does not exist, are wearily irritat- ing in their statement that the town teas seen its day,aed is now on the down grade. It is certainly true that Run- corn, in cemmon with other tewns of toe kingdom, nas suffered r colitiy from acute depression in trede,but it is surele unfair to deduce troua this feet all inherent indica- tion ef permanent decline. Commerce, as we all }thew has its ebbs and fiesve, and to-day's gain may resco-e the loss of vi s-erday. rue varieus trade disputes wnicts of recent years have seriously affected the trade of Use country in g %rare!, have riot bade unfelt in Ruacorn. Tne Peurrisn q sarry strike is a case in point. A good portion of the Penrhyn slates is exported to Ruecern, which consequently suffered severely whilst the quarries were cloessi. And now that they are ence again in full swing. the effect is strekiag. Large consignments are daily retching the post, and the utmost activity pre- vails at the necks, wnere the 4CCOM Xlol4tiOa iS s erely taxed to meet the heavy demand mide upon it. Nor is the West oh England clay trade in a less thriving coadi- tion, and this notwithstaaniug the rival claims of Pres- ton, which, though certainly nearer of access te the great centres of Lancashire, does not possess the same advantages and facilities for dealing wan the traffic as these enjoyed be Rancorn Vessels can only reacts Pres- ten docks at certain statee trinies of the tide, arid the navigation of tee Preeten Cannel is adatittediy weeatis- factory, if not dangerous. But the &sip CokkaAt has tuiw thrown Ritecora open independently of tee tide, and this in itself is an advantage which tells strongly in taveur of the Cneehire port. Then, again, too sea treiehts to Runcorn are considerably lower than they are to Preston, a factor which opera es materially with shippees in these days of keen c nnpetition : wenst valsels chartering to Ruocorn are nearly always sure of an outward car() el coils or salt, the sea freight on which ranges from ss. 61. per ton upwards. Unfortunately for Runcorn, there is uo railway Coln- petitiol. the London and North- Western Comeeny own the only railway on the spot, and they onseereeentiy occupy the pesition of masters of the situati in Lois is the exact opposite of the case at Preston, where the railway company, being couj tint owners of the port, have a direct influence in its welfare. For years past it his bees a matter of strong compiaint at Ruacurn thet the railway company wilfully neglects the int, rests of the port. Oa many occasions the wnole of tie vase trade of the docks is p slyeed by the action of the railway company in tailing to supply a sufficient numb-r of trucks. For days together not ft single truck is available, with the rcsalt that delay to I the traffic takes piece, work is impe 'e I, and trade passes away never to retuin. Tue Ship Canal Company are powerlese, and their elf orte to m tintain the prestige of the port are thus need ered nu eetury. Ire other respec:s the pert of Runcorn is irnpr wing. Accommodation is now provided at the lay-by for vessels of heavy b trthea, whim cergoes can be easily and expe ittiouely urea- shipped into barges for conveyance inland ; and with the further facilities weten the S ip C tua Compaey Promise shortly to in-auliurate, Runcorn, nntwithistanu- in, some of the drawbacks alluded to, rney confidently still hope te hold her own. Every disposition is shown on the part of the Canal Company to meet the growing requirements of the esh pping and commercial interests if the port, and the present able nyeeager of the corn pany (Mr W H Collier), is a man wnose natimate kaowleige of the Bridgewater trades enables him to eitimste fully the advantage likely to result from a , wise and vigorous develepinent of the facilities of the port. LI other directions the present industrial condition of Runcorn affords satisfactory and unmieta.keable evi- dences of expansion and development. In addition t the new industry for the manufacture of quicksilver whicn is about to locate itself in the town, the writer is able to a.nno ince another. The old smelting works are being rapidly reconstructed and fitted up as a rnanufsc- tors f r the rcovereof precious met Lis —an entirely new industry as far as Runeorn is concerned; whilst arrange- ments are in progress which are likely, at no distant dare, to eventuate in the welcome announcement that other works of an imp irtant nature are about to establish their quarters in Ruecorn. The extensive series of new works at the Old Quay are also rapilly nearing com- pletion. The old copper and vitriol works formally con- ducted by Wine, Brothers, and S:eele, and now the pro- perty of the United Alkali Company, Limited, which up to recently were practically closed, have not only been considerably extended, but are now in full swing, whilst other new and extensive plant has been erected'. In close proximiey are the new white lead works,thet promise to become an imp .iirtant industry of Runcorn. The firm is that of the Lancashire (Ma' thews') n hi'" Lead Company, L;mi-ed, who have also a large works in the North of England, and one at Greenock. Tie White lead is manufactured by a patent process, which ,is a distinct impr we n .nt its all respects on the oil methods. The Urban Ceuncil, ever wishful te lift the town into its old position of indeatriel impertanee, are adopting a wise anti enlightened policy. The Cassner- Kellner works at Westnrs Punt have also evid-ntly come to sray,and are materially aiding to the in lustrial importanc, of the district. Some 600 men are employe:l, and further extensions of the works are centemplsted. These, surely, are very gratifying indications that Run- corn has turned the corner of acute depreesiora ; and if the report recently circulated that the United A kill Company centem ulated the rem wal to Wallies ce the Camden Soap Works proves, as mist people think it will, incorrect and without f eundation, nothing in the present condition of t')e town exits to lend colour to any alarmist reports of iniestrial d. c ine.

She then went to the front door, but could see nothing of him She asked a youth named Rskin D ivies if he had seen Walter, and he re- plied " yes, he has just gone down the street." She went down the street ro his tatnPr's house to see if he had gone there, but could not find him. A. anort tines afterwards she heard he was dr owned.—Elsvard Boils a, lock-k_eper, at the Fradshem Locks, states that about 7.15 p.m. on Wednesday, he saw the deceased g Arm past his hotve along the Weaver Canal bank, and when he got to the bridge, about 300 yards past the house, Brett whistled twice. On look.ne round, he sew Brett near the Canal Bridge. Bratt, on seeing him look, at once dived into the canal. Bole e ran up to the spot and saw Bratt's coat and cap on the bank, and called Walter twice, but could not see anything. ifs then ran back to the lonk-house and gat a boat hook, and a "life hook," and with the assistance of Allen Lovett, and his son-in-law, the body WAS reeovered. Information of the occurrence was then given to the police and doctor. On Pollee Constable Price arriving on the scene artificial means oft respiration were resorted to, but although kept up tor aborit an hour were unavailing. Dr. Bennie then ap- pearing pronounced life extinct and the exertions were discontinued. On searching the drowned man's clothes the police officer discovered a note in the j telt it po iket bidding his parents, and brothers and sisters good-bre. —The case has been reporiesi to the Coroner and doubt- less the inquest will be held to-day (Friday).

Taylor. A pre-- gramme of thirty items was gone through consisting of action songs by girls. dialogues, recitations, and slogs by gide and boys. The thrilline story of "The Lifeboat" was well told by Mr. Harry Did las was also "An Ole on Wellington" by Mr. Herbert Unsworth. The room was well filled by an apprecietive and pleased audience. Oranges were given to the scholars at the close. The scholare of the Roman Catholic Schools with their officials and teachers formed its order at Mill Brow School as follows :—St. E iward'e League of the Cross Band, Rev. Father Gore (priest-in-charge and superie- tendeat), Messrs S P Quinn (secretary), J Donnellan, D Doyle, James Caskey, J J Whelan, Misses Barry (teachers), S. Moulsdale, J Dowd, the Children of Mary. Boys of St. Aloysiue and League of the Crose, school cbi dren, and other.. The children tarried a number of beautiful banners, most of the juveniles. being attired in white. The procession moved down Bridge-street, Church-street, Regent-street. Green way-road, Victoria- road, and thence to the scheols, where the scholars were entertained to an excellent repast. The remainder of the evening was spent in games, the elder scholars engaging in dancing to the strains of a band. Numb' rs of the townefelk availed themselves of the cheap trips to North Wales, and the English Lake Dis- trict, and especially the trip to Windermere and More- cambe, instituted by the Liberal Club. Business was generally suspended until Tnursiay. As More ststed the holiday was considerably spoilt by the heavy rains, but some flashes of fan and elopement were obtained "between drops "as it were and who will say they did not enjoy themselves—not an Englishman.

div.head: MANCHESTER PORT SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: MANCHESTER PORT SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The Clerk read the following letter from the Man- chester For Sanitary Anthority (per Mr. J. H. Crocker), dated May 20-h :—The Local Government Board Order coneti:uting the Manchester Port Sanitary Authority expired in March last, but an extension of six months has been granted so that if possible an amicable arrange- ment as to contributians by the various authorities abutting on the Port can be came t, failing this the Local Government Board will make an order compelling certain bodies to contribute. Tue contributing bodies under the old Order were—Manchester 4, Salford 4, Stretford 1. These are willing to contribute as before for the new Order, provided your Aucnority will bear the expense of removal and treatment in laospit at of any dangerous iafectious disease removed from a ship bound for or within your district. The estimated expendi- ture for 1899 is bcween £6OO and £7OO. Arrangements are made with Liverpool to remove any case of small-pox at a charge of four guineas per week, and an annual charge of £llO will be paid for the inspection, removal and treatment of cholera, plague er yellow fewer cases. You are not asked to contribute anything towards this at present excepting in the event of a case of smalp-ix being removel from a ship bound for your part of the port of Manchester when you would have to pay the 4 guineas per week per case. The Port San:- Lary Inspector visits Runcorn and Weston Point di,- tricts twice a week and during 1893 there were 334 ships lop .cted as to their sauitary condition. The Port Medics! Officer visits any case of sickness brought to his notile or any serious insanitary condition of a versel. Arrangements are made with the Runcorn Urban Authority for the removal of infectious cases to their hospital from ships in your district and in an emergency Dr. McDougall visits a suspert sd case under instructions from the Port Medical Officer at a fee of a guinea per visit Per ship- Wiring the two years I isave been meii- cal officer no case of smallpox has occurred on ani snip bouni for your district, the only cases of infection be- ing four cases of typhoid fever removed to Runcorn Hospital last year. I shall be glad if you will brill:: this matter bJore your au'bority at their next meeting, as the Local Government Board are writing on the mattnr." _ _ _
It was unaninnouily decidid to fall in with the 6ug- gestion on the proposition of Mr. Williams, seconded by Mr. Clarke.
THE BATE'S BRIDGE PROPERTY.

Mr. A. Selketd, of Poole Dale, Runcorn, wrote to Mr. Knowles, the Chairman of the Coursed, as follows :—" I beg respectfully to call your a'tention to a report in last Saturday's paper, relative to Dr. A lams' repot uncle eight cottages at Bate's Bridge. This property is owned by an old lady (Mrs. Garniss, of Colly Croft, Ashbourne) and lam the agent here for the property. I think Dr. Adanas must be labouring under some wrong im- pres 1)n, as I Can assure you that the cottages are neither Camp nor insanitary, and after seeing the report (for no information was sent to me), I sent a couple of men to prove the sewers which were found open and in g ood rder. The grid at the tap, which merely takes off the Water Works Company's water was choked up, evidently by children, with stones, and these were at once removed. There is thr iueh ventilation as the windows have recently been opened under the stairs allowing a god current of air to pass from back to front arida considerable sum of money has lately been spent in painting these cottages, puling sop spouting Rec., as suggested by Dr. Adams, and there- fore you can; readily understand the great surprise with which we real the r spert in thus papers, for I vent ore to say this property is far healthier than some town pro- perties, and will compare favourably with any other in Halton. The cases of fever'and diphtheria Dr. Adams will find on closer investigation have not been contracted at the cettages hut elsewhere." The Medical Offi ;et said he hai laid stress upon the continual overfl )sy of sewage into the yard, thnugh the blocking sip of the sewers. He hal never been on the premnes once when the grids and sewerage arrange- ments had been working at all wort sneaking of. The yards had always been overflowed with slops (sr rain water and on his last visit these was a deposit of 21 to 3 inches. It was the sewerage arrangements he complained of. It was perfectly true that when spouts were fixed, some back win lows were put in, but they did not cause through ventilation in the true sense of the term. They were a mere subterfuge and he doubted whether tily were ever used. There was no doubt about the general statement that this was not healthy property ; it could easily be borne ont. Mre:Wright said this question had been before the Hal- ton Parochial Committee, but unfortunately he was not nresent. He had thought it was another property, but now found it was the property belonging to this old lady who was 89 years of age. There had been a large sum of money spent on the property. Since the last meeting he had examined the premises very carefully, and he saw most of the tenants. There were five tsnants in nine house. One tenant had been there for ten years, and never lied ale' sickness in the hnu es. In the house where a child had had diphtheria, the mother admitted tnat she had been away where there was diptherit, and prnb sb'y the child had csueht the disease there. He could 603 nothing very much the matter with the pro- perty except the water. The water tap was in the yard and the children kept turning it on, and he suggested to Mr. Salkeld that kr should place a tap in each helices, and Mr. Salkeld said he would do this if it would be esti.- t-re. Under the circumstances, Mr. Wright moire I that the matter be referred back to the Halton Paro3hial Committee. The Msdical Officer coincided with the proposal to put water tans in the houses if the sewerage were also taken up and thoroughly examined. IMr. Stokes seclndel the proposition, which was carried.
THE lIEDIC&L OFFICER'S REPORT.

Mr. Wri?ht Fiala the rvort must have entailed a tact amount of labour, but h thought in Many eases, the members put it on one side and n9ver re.ld it. Admiral Parry seconded the motion but suggested that a special committee should be appointed and Mr. Wright aorepted this. The Chairman ask ed Dr. Adams if he had any special points he would like the Committee to take up. The Me Mica! Offioer replied that ita his report he had summarised a number ot things which had become dere- lict or urgent or otherwise required attention, and which could not be dealt with in the ordinary fort- nightly reports. Mr. Woo-iward said if a small committee would rernrt to &he Council upon insanitary conditions calling for special attention it would be a benefrcial thing for the district instead of taking them haphazard as they came now from some extraneous source. The motion was carried. The CemmiLtee was constituted of the Chairman, and Messrs. Wright, Mclntyre and Williams.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES,
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES,
LBY I CORREBPoNDENT.

The holiday= are now over, and the town has once more resumed its normal appearance. As I. stated last week, the usual Suoday school proces- sions took place, but the Frien ySociet:es—of which one only had decided to walk—v the last moment were unrepresented. This is the first time in the memory of Runcorn that a Whit-Monday has gone by without a friendly society to enliven its streets.

The Liberal Club had a trip to Morecambe and Windermere, and tho.e who avgiled themselves of the opportunity of going to that pretty splt were fully repaid by the delightful time they 4pent. I hear, however, that the venture was not a- success- ful as it might have been; hut tat must bte ac- counted for by the unfaveurablH weather prevailing. A number of members, who could n't go wlth the trip, complain anti inetly too, that the Club was closed for the day. The holiday is the very day that such a place shoull be open.and the Committee should manage their affurs a little better thau this if they intend catering for the welfare and conven— ience of the members.

I understand that the annuql meeting of the Run- corn Football Club, which takes place on Tues lay next, will be a little livelier than it lias been for some years past. A considerable number of tbe tnemberq feel dispose '• to advocate a slight change in the official reprecentation,which wid not be dis- tasteful to the majority of the members. But I seed say no more only "wait and see."

div.head: AIISTEN-GWELO, ItIiODESIA..
div.p: AIISTEN-GWELO, ItIiODESIA..

Among Rhodesian shares we have frequently called attention to those of the Austen-Gwelo Development Syndicate(Limited),as being well worth attention. As we predicted, they have risen in price, and look like vine; much higher. Durhig the past week they have been largely d^alt in by some of the most impertant members of the London Stock Exchange. and oaing to the excel- lent reports coming lorward b ith by cs.ble and letter from the company's manager at rile mines in Rhodesia, these shares clo,ed better on the week. The total capi- tal of the company is only £53 033 in shares of £l, each fully paid, ani it owns a farm of 6,000 acres and five hundred and seven claims in the best- known and most important gold mining districts of Rhodesia. In addition to tile ab)va very sati,fw.itlry information, intelligence has cline to hand showing that as sinking provels the mines develop greater richness. Arrangements are being made to float one set of these claims as a company, which will eir.ble the Austen (Gwelo) Development Syndicate (Limited) to pay a handsome dividend. Speculative investors might do worse than nick up these share° at the present price of about £2 23 61. at which they are now dealt iu on thet London Stock Exchange.

On Monday afternoon, the annual fête was held at Mr. Thomas Carter's, of Garrett's Parm, The weather was very unfavourable. but there was a coed attendance of people, and the committee, officers, and their assistants, ho,th ladies and gentle- men, did their utmost to make the proceedings as enjoyable as posible. At two o'clortk, the War- rington Borough Band arrived at the Presbyterian school, and a procession was formed of the children and others, nni marched to the farm. Where is my boy to-night"; Bro Wilson 'mouth organ solo; Sister Thomas, solo, "On the. Banks of Allan Water." A vote of thanks was ren- dered to the visitors on the motion of Bro J Sheath. seconded by Sister Sheath and carrled unanimously. Bro Woods. L.D., and Bro Newman, D.S.J.T., and Bro Thomas replied on behalf of the Earlestown lodge. Bro Woods closad the lodge in the usual manner after an enjoyable evening had been spent.

NIEILVIiW- .WITJI. THE .SEC
t.

• .• ; (Cosizapuran.) Anyone • -passing: up, or down the west side of Bridgesstreet and locking along :.Friar's-gate when this narrow street is clear of buildersl carts, hansom; cabs, dour-wheeled carriages and coal carte,; could, not fail ta be-impressed porticoed building that runs at right angles at the end of its short length From the ,windows of this large .b'uilding there stand,, out antarolden characters theniyetic -letters Y.ll.:C.A.andanxious -to solve the meaning these: -four-initials, I Nisited the establishment , with that- _object,- Entering the edifice up font spotlessly clean.stepe, and pushing aside the, glazed door I found myseg -knocking at theldoor of the' .)ssesetary's, office, which; is - only a step from the entrance. In answer to my knock there appeared the persen of the'Secretary himself. I found him ,to a -gentleman almost six feet in. height, of, muscular build and athletic figure; . his appearance 4n-thld litter respect losing- heightened by'a cycling eoStame; Rig aspect; though' inclined to be some- whaV Rein; *delta iutd..k,guiitiTty" during • ccinversa- tiOn, Whe,p, 'his e"y6 apitiklics ind 'a meitry laugh Plays ahOlit ' hie lace. X;seedily ,inafounced to bir„.l,W,indle-,-fer that in the ,u,arge of the secretary-e-the ,object of my mission, and he very. courteously expresse4 his readiness to afford me all the iuformation at his command. He ex- plained to me that the mystic initials-stood for the words "Young Mail's' Christian Association," where- upon I genly 'suggested -that I • had heard that in the minds of' the young men of Warrington the, thied letter carried' a different signification viz.— " rUrglng," AscratzOn AI" said the Sectetaty: , with a gittile;'' Via!' Was in liygone days. It arose in this way: There was a cricket club inconneetion ,with the A.,-,sociatioi4„ and young .men joined the Y.M.Q.A. for the sake of...the,club,whn cared nothing fop:rut:principles, and their ;language .on the field was oftewsuch lacrto bring the Association into dis- repute with the visiting teams, and thus it came to pass that we got an evil reputation." -" What are you doing to;rehabilitate the Associa- tion in the minds of our young men-?" • "It is my endeavour to attract to the Association earnest Christian young men who Will rally round Me end form a central beat of. worker's; to try and nut into opetation the foundation principle of the y.M C.A. ; and I am pleased to say that this plan is succeeding." "What means have you adopted with a view to effecting this object." 'A When Lcame. to Warrington-last. July, to take tip the -work here, I found that there was no, spiritual work carried Sin- 'during the. week, FO idatehdi ney ohnortunity• to 'came:fence a meeting, 'eta spiritu'alhatere: One Tuesday evening about nine o'clock when the Tenniaplayers'were finish- ing play, because of the darkness, I asked three of the Members if they-WoUld meet me uerstairs bra little while for prayer and study of the Bible. They Raid they did not mind, sad so we started a meeting which has since,been held every Tuesday and from this sinall,heginning has grown a class of twenty members, , with an average attendance of twelve:" ," De you find-your memberscinterested in a dull Bible Class ?"- • . . , • Oh, bur-q3ible;Classl .is not a dull affair, by any meads: Why, one fellow said that he would rather Miss his dinner than mtse this ineeting,and I know, aszalatt, that sonie ót the members are as eager to attenßet.the'licini that they • have hardly time to Wash tbeme4vei. . "Then if it is not a daft affair, haw do you con- duct it,?," . i "-My ilea of conducting such a meetinz is to make the ,membera forget that there is a conductor ,present, and that end is attained by-discussion. We 'do not stiek -hard- and fast to the subject in-hand, bile if any member is seeking light-on any other subject the class turns to' the consideration of that subject.' " , ' ' Can' YOU.get the membere to main,tain the die- . a . . cussionr„ do not say that all i' eetings are equally good, but taking.thero all round we find no difficulty in getting,the members to say what they think," , " What is the aim of this weekly meeting ?" "Toe lauilding.up of individual Christian life and I preparing young men for evangelistic work." F " Do. you do any evangelistic work at present?' "No, not at.presene, but we are hoping to begin Work'shrirtly, lfr the open air." • • , "What other agencies have you at work There is on &inlay 'afternoons,' In the Lecture Hall; which, is, proving too 'Small for the numbers attending. Thep in the evening [rein seven An, eight o'clock we have a meeting for young men, who are not attached to any particular church. On Monday evenings we have a small debating class. which is proving very beneficial- to those who at- tend, in helping them to publicly express their opinions' On the first Wednesday in each month there lea nieeting oi the "Regians Beyond Mission- arY Union"' a bratichilaying been formed in con-. nestitin With the Asslciation. The attendences at this meeting are very encouraging, the lest meeting being the best attnded Of any yet held." " Toayhat purpo,e is the hu4cling itself put?"

. , . " First And foremost is our, reading-room, which is supplied with daily and weekly papers, the monthly magazines. and notes and magazines from other Associations, &c. The raiding room also con- tains-a good library of vine 200 volumes. Then we have rooms for conversation; lectures and classes, and on the ground floor there arcrooms-set apart for games. 'The upper portion of the -building is let Off for lodgings for Single members; under the charie of the. car9talser, Mr. George Yeadon. We also.ntilize tne lawn for the . purposes of a tennis club and this recreation„ on ground, in so central a polition, is much appreciated by .the members ot the club. Also, We 'hive just.started a cycling club, which is divided into two. scions, Thursday and Saturday, and is calculatel to bring the members more into communicatian with one atothQr. " Do the raembm.s of the Association avail them- strives of its privileges ?" • "Wt have abl)ut 120. members —and the number 'SteadilV inereasingL--but Owing to many causes they don't come round as I think they ought to do. Anyway they don't. put the same interest into the work as I did when I was an ordinary member at Hull. . , .

"Is the Institute gaff-supporting ?" "No, it -is not, and never will be in one settle because -the membership fees are so low that it is impossiblelo meet expenses by' this means. The emseriuence i that we have to 'appeal to lcical gen- tlemen and Others interested in the spread of Chris- tin work.amo igst young men, for funds to carry on the work ani by the assistance thus obtained I the Association keeps oo its way." " Is tkere any other fact you would like to make I public r !, I should just like to say that the. Association is doinggood work among the young men, especially in the spiritualssphere; During the •wir.ter•months there have been ten cases of conversion among the members and in addition to these there were 36 enquirers 'as the result' of addresses at the Parr anti. 1 regret' very ' much that we have not a gymoasium, as that would ba great, advantage to us in our 'physical department. I regard the spiri- tual work As the most important. ;buy nixt to that comes the physical, for it seems to me that if a man is in poet hodily condition he is very much handi- capped for intellectual pursuits." • . • At the conclusion cf the interview Mr. Windle conducted .me • over the premises, which 1 found light, airy, and well furnished; and juit the sort of place for a' young man to spend his leisure hours amid such society as is calculated to improve his general Well-being.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.

THE REASON OF OUR HOPE. Mr. M. Adams, of Cr we, lectured in the Christadel- phian Room, Bold•str, e', on Sunday, on the above sub- ject, and said the excellent advice given by Peter "to be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hepe that is in you," was not acted on ; at d many paople nad very pronounced objec- tions to dlicuSiluit or controversy on religious subjects. These ohje ,t is Alleged they did not wish to penetrate mysteriee ;a4 secret things belonged to God, but they must not forget, that those things which are revealed, belong unto us, and if they responded to the invitation to reason together, they had in the scriptures (from which Paul reasoned out of), cl,!finite grounds for their hope. The ortuodox hope of heaven going was consoling hut it was unscriptural and delusive—a paean doctrine—and the truth having been supplemereee by fables, the deluted and adulterated doctrines foisted on the churches by the preachers,were accepted, because people d d not examine the Scriptures for themselves. Mores was admonished by God to make tee tabernacle accirdiug to the pattern shewed ta him on the Mount, and there was no more authority for admitting people to heaven in the ant itype, than there was in the type for admitting people into the holy place within the veil. The lecturer asked his hearers not to be beguiled by "the free and easy salvation " or larger hope, which was universalism in a new guise, and was the rebound from the endless torment theery. The truth was between these two extremes, mid to those who were under the fatal delusion that all would come right in the end, be would call attention to Peter's query "If the righteous scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and sinner appear." They were invited to read the glorious promises dependent on Christ's return ti the earth, for those who wore ignorant of those promises (whatever profession they made) were, as the Ephesian Gentiles, "without Christ, being aliens from the Commonwealth lof Israel and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world." Those ,1 who objected that the Jew was dishonest and sordid, !zee appeared to overlook the fact that the Bible draws I attention to their evil character, but the position of Israel at the present time wasA standing monument to the truth of the Bible, and the present movement of the " dry bones "or as one of the notable events preceding the cc ming of Christ,who would purge the evil from the Jews and mske them fit instruments for the subjuga- tion of the world.
THE VICAR OF ST PAUL'S AND TRADES UNIONISM.

In St. Paul's Church on Sunday morniwz, the Rev E R Tarbuck obseived in the course of his sermon that the keen stru4gle now-3-days tended to blunt the moral sense, and make men selfish and careless for the welfare of others. On the whole, however, he thought that we in England were leaving the spirit of competition with some of the spirit with responsibility to others. He trus- ted that trade unions of all kinds might foster that spirit of responsibility, and dot tend to increase the temptation to selfishness. That temptation was too strong now, but public opinion, taught by the nobler mind, was gill on the tight side, thank God, in social matters. He VIVI thankful to find such a large number of persons in that parish willing to devote themselves to direct service in the church—a number that was not only large, but was increasing—and he believed they would yet restore the garish to its brat state of efficiency

div.head: HANDLE OF THE HATCHET.
div.p: THE HANDLE OF THE HATCHET.

I Near me on the table as I write, on the top of a pile of old books, lies a hatchet that looks to be even older than the books. I notice how smooth and worn the handle is, erpecially at the place where it has been so often gripped by 'people in hammering and chopping. The edge is dull now, and the back is flattened and truised, showing what a lot of effective work it has done in its time—all because it is made of good stuff, both bled e and handle. Nobody ever makes the mistake of ever trying to use a hatchet except in one way—taking it by the handle.

What of that, then P you ask me, and why all this jabber about a rusty old hatchet on the t9p of a pile of rusty old Woks. I'll tell you in the twinkling ef a marlinspike. The text is, "T he importance of taking hold of Things by the R ight End," and the sermon there on shall be plain and short, as all the test at rrnors are Now Mrs. Mary Giggens is a lacy who lives at West Tilbury, near the mill, in E, sex ; and she is wIl ard favourably known in the district. An or gtt e many who kncw her is Mr. Bart, the cobras:Er at Wet t Til- bury, and he corroborates every wcrd she says about what happened. Her own story, tut in icw words, is this :—For tong time, man y years in fact, she had been under the harrow with bad health. Her trJuble was the f amiliar and abominable ' c3mplaint, indigestion. Every time he ven:u 01 :o est in i:d than ii n Ire morsel she suffered with pain at the chest and stomach. If you qdon't know what a perfect purgatory of a life this is it is because you have ire ver made the acquaintance of that disordev.

" However," says Mrs. Giggens in her cheerful way of speaking, " I got on fairly well up to the autumn of 1891, when another eo mplaint toAr hold of me. I mean rheumatism, which, if anything, was worse than the in- digestion. It started in my right arm and shoulder and gave me such pain as I had no idea of before. People with rheumatism sometimes call themselves martyrs, and I don't think the word is a bit too strong, for the way this complaint can torment one is something awful. My joints got to be hot and swollen all round, and hurt me so I hardly had any rest with them day or night. "By and by, what with the indigestion and the rheumatism, I got so weak I could neither walk nor do a hand's turn for myself. I couldn't even brush my own hair, nor lift anything. The power seemed all gone out of my right arm. " I was like this for about three years ; and long worrying years they were. If you shculd ask me to de: scribe what I went through I 51aould tell you it wa, quite impossible. Every mouthful of food I took gave me pain at the chest and between the shoulders ; and because of this I ate as little as I could ; and so got weaker and more miserable continually. I consulted doctors and took medicines, and rubbed on ointments and liniments, etc. ,Lut they eased me only a moment as you may say, but thee I would be bad as ever. In February it was (of 1895) I first read about Mother Seigel's Syrup as a great and won derful cure for indiges- tion, and I made up my mind to try it for that, thinking I might bear the rheumatism better if could get rid o the indigeition. So I went to the Intermational Tea Stores at Graves end and bcught a bottle of the Syrup. "In a few days I was a dcal better. There was Ifs pain at the stomach, chest and shoulders, and besides I felt stronger. On this I kept taking the Syrup, and in a little while, to my great surprise and delight, all the rheumatic pains that had troubled me so long disappeared, and I was a new creature. Presently I was strong as ever in my life, and since then I have had no return of either the rheumatism or the indigestion. " What I want particularly to mention,and call atten- tion to is that when I began taking Mother Seigel's Syrup for the indigestion I had no idea of its doing me any good for rheumatism. Yet I feel deeply thankful all the same, and perhaps you will kindly explain the reason why the medicine cured both complaints, as others be- sides me wculd like to knuw. You may print my letter if you wish for the good of other sufferers."—(Signed. MARY GIGGENS, West Tilbury, February 2, 1899. As to the explanation, that we will give blithely enough as we have done many a time before. Indiges" don (because of the poisons it fills the blood with) is the cause of rheumatism. Hence. when Mother Seigel's Syrup had cured the lady's stemach trouble, the rheumatism had to go away with it? Do you see ? Kill a bad cause and you kill a bad effect. Why, la ! me, it was like taking that old hatchet by the handle instead of by the blade. But hatcht-ts are easier to under stand than diseases arn't they ?
GOLF.

div.head: SABBATH: IS IT SUNDAY?
div.p: THE SABBATH: IS IT SUNDAY?

was much pleased with the letter of " lona " in last i6SUO on tire Sabbath. If that letter tends in however small a degne be lessen Sunday labour of man or beast it will have accomplished a gooi work and one at which all right feeling people must rejoice. I quite believe with him that compulsory Sunday labour is both a dasger and a diserace to our country, and should be discouraged as much as possible. So far lam with him and wish him God speed; what amaz,s ma is his cock-sureness abut everything. Indeed his letter has one phrase conspicuous for its absence, which would add very materially to irS value— " One never knoss." Its tone is that of an active participant in the pre-mundane Council ; for does he not tell us " the day of rest " "is as old as the world itself ?'' Herein, surely, he has forgotten his geology. To the ordinary,or garden, mind, it would seem that the Dinoserium, Labyrinthotion and other animated forms of the pre-hurran habitan's of the world would need no Divine injunction to rest. It is very re- freshing to read " lona ;" n ) doubt or hesitancy about him- Indeed I should say his favourite poet would be he who wrote Oh I never, never let us doubt, Things which no one can be sure about." When next he favours us with a line would he kindly tell us how it is, if "God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it," and "the law of the Sabbath . . . is not subject to abrogation or revision by men "—will he say how it comes about that, it has been both revised and abrogated as to its date ; changed from the s-venth to the first day of the week. Can he find any Divine in- junction to do this ? Yours &c., JOHN PEERS.

div.head: CYCLING.
div.p: CYCLING.

rW. Collin has been riding to good purpose this week and his early: successes promise well for his form this season. On Bank Holiday, at Bangor Sports, he gained the premier prize in the one mile roadster bicycle handicap from scratch, and in the two-mile bicycle race from 15 yards. He was also second in the one-mile bicycle race. On Saturday Collin carried off the third prize in the two miles bicycle race at Poo!stock, Wigan.

-4 On Wednesday evening, there was offered for sale at the Co-verative Hall, before a numerous com- pany, 12 lots of shop and cottage property, situate in Wargrave-road, owne-1 by Mr. A. L. Collings. of lace, and formerly of Earlestown. Tflo premiss were first offered as one let, and commencing at £2,000, the bidding advanced slowly to .£2,700, at which price they were withdrawn. They were then oft-red in single lots, but as no bids were forthcoming, the sale wai declared closed. EARLESTOWN MISSION.

In connection with this Mission, a pic-nic took place on Monday to Chester. Although the morn- ing was so unpropitiow, about 50 of the friends connected with the Mission left Earlestown by the 8.46 train, and reached Chester shortly before 10 o'clock. The weather improved somewhat duriniz the afternoon, and the party ware enabled, without inconvenience to visit the various places of inter- est, including the Mitrket Hall, Museum, Barr3ck4. Park,and Cathedral,where some of the party avtiled themselves of hearing service. The arranemews were in the hands of Mr.R. Macklin, assisted by 4r. J Liatherbarrow and Mr.J. Singleton,and they were heartily thanked for the enjoyable outing they had provided. The party reached home about 10 o'clock. GOOD TEMPLARY.

The usual weekly meeting of the Hope of Earles- town lodge of Good Templars lwas held in the Co- operative Hall, Wargrave-road, )n M milay evening Bro Cutler P CT, presided. Bro J W olds proposed a member to be received as an ancient l'emplar, which was duly acceded to. Bro Woods also gave notice of the District Loige meeting to be held at S'arnport, and read letters from Bro Stonehouse,of Liverpool, offering to read a paper on "Diana of the raphesians," and " Bacchus of the 11, iish," on July 24th, and from the Temperance Mission lodge, War- rington, inviting the Hope of Earlestown to pay them them a visit. The report of the Programine Committee was adopted with slight alteration. The programme for the evening was carried out, under the presidency of Bro Anderton, the following tak- ing part, Bros Newman, Hobbs, Ballet, Woods, Cutler, Sisters Thomas, Woods, Croft and Owen. T. JOHN'S CHURCH SUNDAY ::CHOOL, EIRLESTOWN. The annual picnic in connection with the teachers and officers of St. John's Sunday School, took plice on Monday. About 40 persons journeyed in wagonettes to Frodsham, leaving Earlestown abotv half-past nine, reaching their destination three hours later,the enjoyment ot the drive being greatly marred by the inclement weather. The head- quarters of the party was made at Mrs Parkers, Overton Hills On the way up lunch was partaken of at the "Ring o' Bells." Shortly before sitting down to tea the Vicar,Rev. T. R. Matthews,presented on behalf of the teachers, a gold albert, to the Rev. F. Shirtcliffe, the curate, in appreciation of his management of the preparation classes for teach-rs which he had conducted for the last 18 months. Mr Shirtcliffe made a suitable response, and thanked the teachers for their kindness. An excellently served knife and fork tea was partaken of at 4 o'clock, and the return journey was commenced at, 6 30., home being reached at 9.30. The arrange- ments were in the hands of Mr. Martindale and Miss Egan, who gave seisfaction to all. INTERESTING WEDDING AT EARLESTOWN. The Wesleyan Chapel, at Earlestown, was well filled on Wedneslay afternoon, on the occasion of the marriage of Miss May Clare, second daughter of Mr. Thomas Clare, Claremont. Earlestown, with Mr. Thomas Oarlock, principal of the firm of Stretch and Oarlock, general drapers, of Nantwich. The bride, who is well known in Earlestown, having for many years been principal soprano in the Wes- leyan Church choir, looked very becoming in a dregs of cream silk, trimmed with chiffon, and carried a bouquet of lilies of the valley and roses. Her bridesmaids were Miss Mary Clare and Miss Olive Clare' each of whom was attired in pink and white muslin, trimmed with chiff na. The marriage ceremony was performed by the Rev. George Ham- mond. of Eccles, assisted by the Rev. P. R. Pass- more' and the bride was given away by her father. The service was fully choral, and Miss Greenall, who presided at the organ, played Mendelssohn's "Wedding March." A reunion was afterwards held at the house of the bride's father, and the happy couple afterwardslleft for TAandudno. Tne presents, which were numerous, were of a weful character, including a gold diamond and ruby brooch from a ew friends of the congregation. WHITSUNTIDE AT EARLESTOWN AND gEWTON. A more miserable Whitsuntide than that which prevailed at Earlestown and Newton, and which was evidently general all over the country, could not very well be imagined. The men employed at the Viaduct Works, and Vulcan Founary, might well congratulate themselves that it had been de- cided not to close the respective works on Whit- Monday. Of course t e Vulean men reserve their holidays until August, but the tlen at the Viaduct Works will take their holidays this week erel,when it is hoped there will be some improvement in the weather. The school children are also fortunate in having their annual procession postponed, and this it has been decided will take place on Saturday IJune 10th. All the tradespeople closed their estab- lishments on Monday, and there was a cessation of work at Messrs. Blee and Cos. and Messrs. McCor- quodale and Cos., but the drenehing rain put all idea of outdoor excursions out of the question. A. good number of people however,journeyed tolvarious places, such as Manchester, and Liverpool. despite the rain, but they wore a bedraggled appearance when they returned home.

The weather on Bank Holiday was the cause of much disappointment. Rain fell heavy and con- tinuously throughout the day, but despite that. fact, many left the town. The following were the princi- pal bookings from tie two stations :—Bank Quay: Chester. 150; Blackpool, 140; Frodsham, 120; Con- way, 80; Birmingham, GO ; and North Wales, 50. Central: Manchester, GOO ; Liverpool. 900; Long- sight (Belle View), 150 ; Southport, 250. The total number of passengers from the Central was 6,000, a sligta advance upon last year. WARRINGTON AND BANK QUAY SAILING CLUB The first model yacht regatta in connection with this club, was sailed in the Sankey Canal,at Sankey Bridges, on Saturday and was a complete success. Twenty-three boats were entered to compete in the three different classes, five in the two feet class, nine in the three feet, and nine in the big class. The races were sailed off in heats of two and three, a semi-final and a final. The first and second in each class were .-1, Pastime, E Jones owner, and 2, the Alice, E Gleave in the two feet class ; 1, Fairy, It Bunt:tem, and 2. Griffin, R Woods, in the three-feet class; and in the big class, 1, Thistle, J Jackson, and 2, Spray. W Ray. There were some very Close finishes, five seconds only dividing the Fairy and Griffin, and two seconds dividing the Thistle and Spray. The distance sailed was 450 yards, and the course was lined with spectators. The starter was Mr. Fair Turner, and the judges, Mr. J. Hough and Mr. J. Haywood.

div.head: CRUSH THE TRUST.
div.p: CRUSH THE TRUST.
BY Ma. II WHIT/ELM.

A few weeks ago the 16 Examiner," had a short editorial :on the possibility, or otherwise, of the Standari Oil Company, of America, having influ- ence sufficient to prevent a Bill fr.irn passing in the 11lus:.1 of Commins. such Bill having Lir its oh- Iset the imposing of a flash test for oil used for do- mestic purposes. It is quite likely a considerable nuuaber of readers would pass over the editorial referred to as soms- thing of not much moment, and therefore requiring 'no further thought. Allow me to say that few _

more important -questions have, wain recent years, called; for the attention of the House of Com- mons, and the English constituen6e,s than thu one I refer to. In a word, the present flush test for illu- minating oil in Knglind is from 25 to 30 degrees lower than it is in America, although the same oils are used in the two countries, that is American oil is used This means, the American oil is sent out to England:in a more impure, and cheaper state than it would be allowed to be sold to the American consumer. Consequently you have more deaths through lamp accidents, pr thousand of population, than we htsve in Amerca. When read the report of the defeat of the measure, I thought there was something more in it than ap- _

peered on the surface. A year or two ago I for- warded to your Free Library a blok, ' Wealth versus Commonwealth." I know not how many of my old townsmen have read it, but I may state that the book is as complete a history,up to date of the American Standard Oil Company as can be made, amd proves pretty conclusively " that for ways that are da,k " the Standard 0,1 Company "takes the cake." It seems the Hotise of Commons was in some sense influenced by a desire to deal in a friendly manner with the United States. Tnis is all hurnbag, or, if there is any truth in it, that truth is based upon a wretched misapprehension of the whole bu-ines. I have neither time nor splee o deal with this matter as ,t should be dealt with. I have no doubt your own member was on the side of the minority when this measure was thrown out, and would, consequently, be quits willing to give his constituents:his opinion on the matter. I should like to read it. Leaving this portion of the subject of Trusts I invite your readers to look up the' Cont,,,mporary Review" for August, 1893. In it they will find an article entitled "The defeat of the Oil Sings." It is signed by Robert Donald, and proves pretty conclu- sively that this Trust has tamp-red wiih the Scotch oil manufacturer,, and, if inference is worth any- thing, it wluld not leave the British 1-louse of Com- mons as pure as one would wish it to be. The caption at the head of this letter is one that is appearing now, almost daily, in the democratic press of the States. It is urged by the party that in the Trust labour has its most deadly enemy, and that it should be crashed. Certainly Trusts are in- creasing to a most surprising degree. Almost every- thing that we eat, drink, or wear is now manipu- lated by a trust. It is sated that Wall-st. turns out twenty trusts a week, and appended here is a sample of one day's work :
ONE DAY'S TRUST CROP.

Dollars. Champagne Trust 50,030.000 TC Forged-Steel Joint Trust ... lOO.OOO Oil Stove Trust Fish and G me Trust Varnish Trust 33,000,000 Thre•hing Machine Trust • Upper Leather Trust 53.000.0n0 • Banana Trust
Window Glass Trust 24,000.039 Paint Trust Scheel Furniture Trust

Of course there is a large amount of inflAtion in all this syndicate floating, and a day of reckoning will come. The plants and good-will of small com- panies are being bought at extravagant prices. The husine4s in each transaction, after going through the hands of the Wall-street brokers, is turned over to the gullible public that seems to be swallowing it rather voraciously. Some outrageous instances are given by the press as examples of the extent to which 1 the w ttering of stock is going on. To those who make the labour question a study the only feature about all this, is, how will it affect wages? Is the employer a rogue and a scoundrel who forces his employes to create profit on inflated stock? Some ot these qubstions will belanswerad before five years are over. Several of the big Trusts are not of the kind just referred to. They are gigantic combinations of wealth, prepared to go to any extent in any country, and with any parlia- ment. Take the sugar trust. It proposes to con- trol the entire sugar trade of the c;)untry,and either put the indeoendents'out of business entirely or make them joln the huge combine. To do this the Trust will reduce its dividends, and, if necessary suspend them. _

Within the past year, and more especially during the latter three months, I have come across a con- siderable amount of literature that seems to have been written especially for the workman's benefit. The writers seem to enthuse, and work themselves lip to a white heat, in their eagerness to press upoe the workman the great necessity that exists for him to be as honest, as expert, and speedy as pos- sible in all his engagements Religion is even drawn in, and the worker is tot I that in Christianity only can he find the help he needs. Why is all this trouble being taken to so impress the worker with his responsibilities ? is "The man with the hoe" the only one to bear the white man's burden? De- pend upon it the burden the white man is now hsine called upon to bear is a burden of his own creating and he need not go over sele to find it. It is said, and has bean said for years that compe- tition is the life and soul of trade. It is urged that the killing of it would reduce us all to one dead level. These are the stock arguments against socialism. It is now an every day oleurrence to see the statement made that competition is ruining prices, and that something must be dsne to put a stop to it. What this something may be in the future one cinnot say; what it is to—lay is easily to be seen. Big oc,an st3amers to reduce cost on freight. Big companies to reduce cost of manage- ment, cost of production,and bring about the death of competition. You have in Birmingham,England, a splendid object lesson now before you as to what reducing cost means in the discharge of hundreds of workmen through the sudden action of the Big Copper Trust. Economy is the order of the day,and what of the workman ? There is quite an amount of gush and sentiment introduced into the discus- sion of this question. May, be the present writer does a little in this way.llowever this may be there is no gush about the fact that 1,000 miners have just taken a ton and a half of dynamite on a stolen train to Wariner, (Idaho.) There they blew tin the great Bunker Fiill Mills to atoms. So far I know of only one life being lost. The object of the men, who were on strike, was to prevent the work from being carried on by non-union men. It is said on all sides, that America is just enter- ing upon such a period of pnsperity as she never yet has seen. Trade is to boom to such a degree. that the land is to overfbw with milk and honey. Already, it is said, wages are being raised all through the eastern states. I read in one trade paper of 38/ per cent, being paid by a cotton com- pany in the south ; its maximum wage paid is 41 a day. I fear dynamite as a force will be tried as a remedy outside of Idaho, unless somPbedy's conscience quickens. Al- though I have used the words "Crush the trust" I feel that it is altogether impractical. In the first place there is no law whereby the Federal Courts can take action, and state laws are altogether use- lees. I regard these huge combines as a natural outcome of past trade conditions. In other words they are a feature in trade evolution, and while they may put a stop to uncontrolled competition they have certainly brought about as great reduc- tions in the price of all kinds of manufactured arti- cles in the United States since their advent as be- fore the tendency to combine became so pro- nounced. I see it stated that the formation of Trusts is increasing as rapidly in Great Britain as in the United States. If this he true, it will be at once apparent that they are not an outcome of protec- tion but are as likely to be fostered in free trade England as anywhere else. Trusts have come to stay for a time. It will be difficult to frame a law that will down a Trust that will not also interfere with the working of an ordinary company. We must therefore reckon with the Trust as one of the important factors in every day life. They will make themselves felt in the smallest details of domestic life as well as in the mighty traffic of the city screets. If we take, as an instance, the familiar household article of baking powder, all competi- tion is stopped. No newspaper ads, no travellers are now requirsd. Now you pay your money and take the article the Trust supplies. Similar results always follow the formation of these modern enter- prises. Economy of production will not always mean greater cheapness in distribution. The cheap- ness 80 far has been a question of policy, done to down the other man. The Trust will drive the

small manufacturer, merchant, and small corpora- tion out of buyiness. What will become or them, especially the small tradesman! All cannot retire on a comfortable competeace. It is sail that a better arttele,lower prices, steady employment, and better wages will follow. This cannot be, as, in each case, inflation of the stock is the rule, and where ' watered sock s and bonds run a factory lower wages, and inferior articles must result. I have no hesitation in saying the immediate result of the Trust will be t 3 sharply divide the people into two classes, masters and slaves. The tendency of the Trust will be to place all business in the hands of a few men, whose main ability is to make money. I see one financial authority says the capital stocks of the Trusts 113 W in existence, amount to nearly six thousand millions of do!lars. Another financial authority says that two thousand five hundred tad- hoes of dollars of this is the capital of Trusts born since January Ist, 1898. It follows this statement with the startling one that one thousand seven hun- dren and fifty millions, out of the two thousand five hwirlred millions represents" water."

The copplr ['rust is the one just now mut pro- minent before the public eye. It is said to have a capital of £40,000,000. Talk of anarchy, socialism &c., &c.,why, the wildest dreams of any, or of all the is,nas' could not accomplish what the Trusts are likely to bring about in a very few years. San Francisco.

Mr. THORNTON drew the attention of the Council:to that portion of the minute relating to expenses specially allowed by the Council. He wanted to know whether it was necessary to insert that. Tilo CLERK Slid it meant Mr. Thompson might be called upon to goo Liverpool or London in which case his eKpensus would be allowed by the Council. Mr. THORNTON accepted the resolution and the minutes were approved on the motion of Mr. Ebughton seconded by Mr. Thornton.

TEE CORPORATION BILL—ANOTHER CLAUSE. Tho CLERK !Rid In regard to the bill before the House of C mirnons, promoted by the Warrington C)rporation, it would affect the wells at Croft which sapplie 1 the in- habitants. In accordance with the Council's resolution and instructions, the Chairman and himself waited upon the Town Clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle), and the Water Envineer (Mr. Dees), at the Town Hall. They were met with every courtesy and when they represented what effect he Bill would have regard- in, the wells, the Town Clerk at once consented, so far- es he was concerned, to introduce a clause in the Bill to protect the wells and promised the clause should be put before his committee sod upon their approval he would send a copy of the clause to him (.11r.Sutton). No clause had come to him (the speaker) up to noon that day,so he sent a clerk to the Town Clerk to say ttat if the clause had not beers written he (the Town c;erk) sinuld write him on the subject. The Town Clerk replied that since the interview he had not had a meeting of his Parliamentary Committee, but he had drafted out a clause to the effect that if the propo3ed works of the Corporation diminishes the supply of water in the wells at Croft the Corpora tion would make good such deficiency, and he had no doubt the Corporation would agree to this. The CHAIRMAN said it was very satisfactory. _

Mr. TILORNTON th3llZht it vrouid be best tops s a re- solution since there had evidently been some mistake i n this omission, and with reg Ar-4 ti other places equally concerned with Croft. He would wive— The Camitxt&N : Thlt would necessitate another in- terview.

Mr. THORNTON Weight not. THO CLERIC asked it Poulton was suppled with water by any och, r rn-ans than wells. Mr. Tilossn. : Yes, Warrington , ater. The CLERK said in Croft they were not suppli,d with any water by the Corporation, and if the wells were taken away they would have no other water. In Pout- ton-with-Fearnhead the Corporation had already laid pipes for a supply of water, and they would not in- deEnnify them. They would say to their Council, that it was their duty to see that their own people were sup- plied. In case of the supply being by wells the matter should be Fettled through a saliciter. Mr. THORNTON thought the District Council should protect the district. The CLF.RK said they were not respsnsible for the supply of water to a parish if it could obtain water by a public supply from the Corporation. Mr. THORNTON suggested that the addition he had mentioned should be made.

Tho CLERK said he wouti try but he did not want to rush the matter and spoil the present COECOS6O[I. Mr. KriowLas said they had had the experience of asking for to) much and getting nothing. A lesion af thot sort should teach them something. Mr. THORNTON said this case was net analagous to the one Mr. Knowles was referring to. It was decided that the Clerk should write to the Town Clerk and sea what he could do in reference to the matter.

The death-rate from zymetic diseas s was 2•1 against 1•0 the average of the last three months and nil the corresponding month of last year. Of 9lthe deaths only one had occurred under the age of one year. The Compu!sory Notificatien Act showed there had been 3 instaNces of scarlet fever.
The report was adopted. GREAT SANKEY. -TRH REPAIR or FOOTPATHS.

Mr. liat:rox, referring to the footpaths in Great Sankey.said he did not know whether their ClErk wuLd agree with him, but according to the remarks of mem- bers of that authority (Great Sankey Parish Council) the Rural Council were legally bound to keep the foot paths in repair. Mr. THORNTON : Who Rail an?

Mr. HALTON : I said so. (Laughter.) Continuing, Mr. HALTON said, as a matter of fact he knew their clerk did not agree with him. Mr. Knowles had written a letter to the Pariah Council at Great Sankey, and, practically speaking, Mr. Knowles was withful to close all the footpaths in Great Sankey. He had be ,n requested by the Great Sankey Parish Council to bring this matter before them. He would like to say that the Parish Count.il thought they (the Rural Council) were legally bound to keep the footpaths in order. The CLERK said he did not think there was any legal binding upon them. He thought that their surveyor would be more competent to speak upon the matter hiving had more experience in those matters. The CLERK suggested that the proper way for Mr. Halton to bring this matter before them was to give notice about the Rural Council undertaking the repair of a certain footpath and the question would then arise about others.
Mr. HALTON brmally gave notice. This was all the business.

div.head: ST. HELENS DISASTER. BOARD OF ifT,TITE INQUIRY.
div.p: ST. HELENS DISASTER. BOARD OF ifT,TITE INQUIRY.
HOW THE EXPLO3ION OCCURRED.

Colonel Ford. C. 8., cbet iuspctor of explosives for the Home o:fice, on Thursday morning heU an inquiry ander the Explosives Act into the recent explosion at Kartz's works, St. Helens. Toe Alkali Company were represented by Sir David Gamble, Mr. T. W. Stewart, general manager, Mr. klfred Gasket', Al4erman J. C. Gamble. Mr. A. Carey, general secretary, Mr. Muspratt, Mr. Hawkins solicitor, Dr. Bet, and Mr. A. Etudge, works manager. There were also present Professor Dupra, Hoare Office expert ; Mr. S. Gloves, Corporation Gasworks manager ; Messrs. H. Rowlinson, Morrison, (Widnes), S. Hillinsworth, G. J. C. Broome, and others. Colonel Ford said the inquiry would be informal, the evidence not being t tken on oath. Mr. Hawkin said he had witnesses preseat, and would call probably the most interesting ea, woo saw the fire break out.

William Batl. cooper. said he had boon employei at the works eight 'ear. A the time the fire broke out he was unloadine a truck which had ben put opposite the door of the crystallising department. He was receiving casks from the driver when he was in the waggon and put them on the floor, in order to take them into the crystallising room. He put two ca9lts down on their side, and then took another cask down and rested it with one end on the casks and the other end on the floor. The weight of the two casks caused the other to roll over, and it rubbed against another. Immediately this happened asp k flew out, and al rnIA simultane aly a flame shot out and ran along by the side of the tank. He gave an alarm. The casks had come from the ceatral cooperage.

div.head: -WHERE THE CASKS CAME FROXI.
div.p: -WHERE THE CASKS CAME FROXI.

Willi ma Brady, foreman c.aopor, sail he was in the cry4allising house receiving the casks from tho last witness. lie heard an alarm, and saw the bottom of the cooler on fire. He alarmed the mon ita the other part of ths refinpry. He knew that the casks came from Bryant and May's. They were 53wt. c tsks, and they ha Ino Itaops on. The casks wore afterwards cleaned and brushed out moat carefully by the poopie who brought the chlorate. He c mid not see any chlorate in the Tho casks were trst lined with paper before the chlorate was put in.

div.head: MANA.GrER'S STORY.
div.p: MANA.GrER'S STORY.

Dr. Best, chemist and manager t Flardshaw Brook rks,which adjoin the scene of the explosion, gave a very vivid description of the explosion. His atteltion was called on the morning in question to large volumes of smoke passing over the railway from the direction of Kurz'e chlorate refinery. He ran to the waste bank close to the door of the refinery. He saw the fire blaz- ing inside the crys:allising house. This room was full of wooden tanks,in which the chlorate was cooled. The fire was spreading from tank to tank,and the place wss full of smoke. He told the men who were wearing the clothes provirfed far the workers in the chi )1-ate house to get away as far as possible, as they were in danger of firing. He had more hosepipcs put onovith toe ebicct of trying to keep tho fire from spreading to the adjoining coopery and wagon works. The fire was runninz along, and caught the roof of the house where the chlorate was packed in the wooden casks. After burning through the roof, the ire spread to the casks. He saw there was no chance of saving the building. The fire worked its way down to the pyramids of c isks within three feet 6f the ground. Then he and all the men with him commenced to run. The flames were treneedous, and the heat from tlym forced the men back 25 yards. Then came a huge roar as if the buildings and their contents were bufst- ing. This caused them to run further distance of 40 yards, when they stopped to look round. The explosion then occurred, and they saw the whole mass go up into the air. He was thrown to the ground. He got up and looked round for the men with him, and he saw they were safe.

div.head: AFTER THE EXPLOSION.
div.p: AFTER THE EXPLOSION.

Over the plaoe where the chlorate house had b33n there was an enormaus white cloud, with a dense mass burning in ths cmitre This was carried over in the direction of Hardshaw Brook Chemical Works. He thought the boiler must have exploded as well, and he went to the place to see. He there met the foreman of t he Flardshaw Brook works,who told him that the vitriol chainbar had gone. He thought the works were on fir 3, but when he got to the place he saw they had only collapsed. He went to the telepheee and spoke to the office. Afterwards he give instruntions that a search should he made for the two men whom he knew were working under the vitriol chamber. The last he saw of the vitriol kegs before the explosion was when the fire had got down close to the ground The pyramid of casks wonld be about fifleen feet in heiaht. Samuel Glover, manager of the Corporation Gas Works, said at the time of the explosion he was going into the gas holder. His attention had been previously railed to the fire,wnich he saw was a serions one. Before he got t the gas holder the explosion had occurred. The force of the explosion, together with the smoke and burning material, travellel in the direction of the gaso- meter. The effect of the explosion, besides bringing down the vitriol charnbsr at Hardsnaw Brook, was evi- dene-d on No. 1 gas holder, the side of which was burst, and the holder was ripped right across the top. This holder at the time was three parts full, and stood about 45 feet high. The secone holder, on the other side, was, fortunately, lower than Na. 1, and was thus protected from the explo4on. When till gas holder was ripped open the gas went up into the air,and burned out in one huge flame, being twice as high as the chemical chim- ney.

div.head: KURTZ'S MANAGER GIVES EVIDENCE.
div.p: KURTZ'S MANAGER GIVES EVIDENCE.

Mr. A. Rude, managr of Khrtz's w ,rks, said the quantitv of chlorate of potash in th store•houst, was about 156 tons, in cwt. casks, beioheing to Messrs. Bryant and May. Wheh the accident hanpehed he was about 800 yards away from the scene. From this point he saw a quantity of smoke issuing from near the re- finery. A man who was with him at the time said it was only steam from the I icomotive. But the smoke rapidly changed colour, and he re ilised that it was the fire from the chlorate refinery. Fie ran to the place, and just as he came round the corner of the waste heap the explosion occurred. :That was within five or six minutes from the time that he first saw the small quantity of Pm )ke. They had found charred staves beloncring to the kegs at a distasce of 300 or 400 yards. There were fund on both siclea of the wo•ki, hut the quantity in question was trifling compared with the number of casks in the storeh,its,. The works and the contents were dissipated by the explosion. Col. Ford slid that they had had no explanation as to how the spark came to fly by the kegs from the barrel which the witness Bate was handling. Mr. Hawkin said that he could gve no other explana- tion as to how the spark was generated beyond what the man told him, as he sail the kegs had moved along and rubbed against one another, and so the spark had been struck.
Cll. Ford astkei if anyone else walt3d to give any evi- dence or eay anything ? There being no response, the inquiry was concluded.

THE EMIGRANT'S RETURN. "Too late, too late," the lady-seid, And watched his darkening brow; "It is too late, my heart is changed, I cannot love thee now For he had been to foreign lands, Had crossed the ocean wide, And had returned in hope, that she, Would be his happy bride. Sadly he gazed upon her face In maiden bloom PO fair, And uttered from his broken heart, In accents of despair ; "Vain, vain the gold I gathered, In rieh Golcondas' mine, If all my hope and fears in life May not be shared with thine." Forlorn he wandered o'er the W*lrld A stranger on the earth Now seemed no longer dear to him The land that gave him birth. For she who had inspired his soul In every change of life, Ah cruel fate she soon would be Another's darling wife. Why did he wander oer the earth And cross the stormy sea ; Why leave her severed from his lave And hope she his would be? Unchanged by time, in heart the same, And deaf to pleadings near, Why cherish the delusive hope He would remain most dear. S. KENYON. Warrington.

PADGATE. A PLUCKY POLICEYAN.—P.C. Clark. of the Lancashire 1 County Constabulary, (stationed at Martinseroft, wkilst on duty the other day in Glazebrook-lane, Rixton, saw a 'runaway horse, attachad to a trap, belongin ta Mr. Peter Leigh, grocer, Warrington. Tee offierar seeing the danger which a number of small children were in, made 1 a plucky effort to stay the mad career of the runaway. He jumped at the horse's head, roizing it by the neck and nose, and at last succeeded in bringing it to a stand- still, thus averting a terrible accident. 1 Tea PARTY.-0q Whit Menday afternoan Mrs. George Mather, of Cinnamon-brow Farm, Fearnhead, gave her annual tea party to all the children residing in the town. ship of Haughton. They assembled at the farm about three o'c!ock, with a number of Mr. and Mrs. Mather's invited friends, and enjoyed themaelves in various ways until about four otelo-k, when they sat down to an ex- cellent tea under the hay shed. Ora account of the wet weather they could not, as usual, go into a field for games and sports for prizes, but enrged in them in the large farm yard and under the hayshed. Nuts and sweets were distributed during the evening, and Mr. and Mrs. Mather did heir utmost to promote tha happi- ness of the children. At dusk hearty cheers were given for Mr. and Mrs. Mather. sad the children separated. MERSEY LODGE DRUIDS' PIC-NIC. About 20 officers and members of the Mersey Lodge of the Ancient Order of Druids of Warring- ton had a waggonette drive to the Joiners' Arms Hotel, Croft, on Saturday afternoon and they met some of the members of the Croft lodge of the order. Shortly after their arrival, they went to the bowling green at the hotel,which was in good con- dition, considering the unfavourable weather, and commenced a main of bowls. At five o'clock, the Warrington party sat down to a knife-and-fork tea, capitally catered for by Mr. and Mrs. S. Dimon, the host and hostess. Afterwards bowling was again resumed until about eight o'clock, when the War- rington party returned borne. The others bowled until dusk, and afterwards a pleasant evening was spent.
